articles.title: Why US is questioning Pakistan's Rs 3 trillion defence spending
articles.summary: The US state department has flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending, while also
articles.body: The US state department has flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending, while also raising concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing the executive budget proposal.The concerns were highlighted in the 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report, which assessed Pakistan's public financial transparency and identified gaps in the country's budgetary and fiscal disclosure practices.The report noted that Pakistan made its enacted budget and end-of-year financial statements widely available online. However, it said military and intelligence budgets remained outside adequate parliamentary or civilian public scrutiny.“The military and intelligence budgets were not subject to adequate parliamentary or civilian public oversight,” the report said.The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period.According to the assessment, this limits the time available for lawmakers and civil society to examine government spending before the budget is adopted.US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparencyThe state department called for three key changes to Pakistan's fiscal transparency framework.It urged Islamabad to make its executive budget proposal publicly available within a reasonable period, disclose detailed information about government debt obligations, including liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises, and bring military and intelligence agency budgets under parliamentary or civilian public oversight.The report also raised concerns about Pakistan's disclosure of public debt, saying only limited information was available on debt obligations, including those of major state-owned enterprises.At the same time, the US assessment acknowledged some positive aspects of Pakistan's public financial system.It said the country's supreme audit institution met international standards of independence and noted that its audit reports were published in a timely manner and contained substantive findings.Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillionThe US assessment comes against the backdrop of a substantial increase in Pakistan's defence allocation for the 2026-27 financial year.In June, Pakistan's federal government proposed allocating Rs 3 trillion for defence services, up 17.65 per cent from the previous year's initial allocation of Rs 2.55 trillion, according to Dawn.The proposed defence services allocation amounts to about 2.08 per cent of Pakistan's projected GDP of Rs 143.6 trillion and nearly 16 per cent of the federal government's total outlay of Rs 18.77 trillion.Spending on civil works related to military infrastructure was projected to rise 7.92 per cent to Rs 363.16 billion, from Rs 336.49 billion previously.Military pensions are accounted for separately from the main defence services budget. The government has allocated Rs 822 billion for retired military personnel under the federal pension outlay, according to Dawn.The allocation for defence administration was set at Rs 10.9 billion, compared with Rs 7.9 billion in the outgoing fiscal year's original budget. That allocation was later revised to Rs 11.75 billion.Major military imports and defence acquisitions are generally funded outside the main defence services allocation and remain undisclosed.The US state department's assessment therefore highlights a distinction between Pakistan's publicly disclosed defence allocation and the wider military spending that may not be fully visible through the country's budgetary documents.Defence spending remains a key transparency concernThe state department's recommendations focus on bringing military and intelligence expenditure into the broader framework of public financial oversight.While the report recognised that Pakistan publishes key budget documents, it identified defence and intelligence spending, debt disclosure and the timing of budget publication as areas requiring greater transparency.The recommendations would require Pakistan to give lawmakers and the public greater visibility into military and intelligence allocations, as well as government liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pakistani minister in Balochistan province escapes armed attack on convoy
articles.summary: Balochistan home minister Mir Ziaullah Langove escaped unharmed after armed attackers targeted his convoy in Mastung district on Friday, injuring six
articles.body: Balochistan home minister Mir Ziaullah Langove escaped unharmed after armed attackers targeted his convoy in Mastung district on Friday, injuring six people, including three police personnel.The attack took place in the Khad Kocha area as Langove was travelling from Quetta to Kalat, Balochistan government spokesperson Shahid Rind said."Six people were injured in the attack, but the minister remained unhurt and the convoy has returned to Quetta," Rind said.All six injured people suffered bullet wounds, according to a senior police official. Three of them were police personnel, with two reportedly in serious condition. They were taken to a hospital in Quetta for treatment.The attack has raised fresh security concerns in Khad Kocha, an area that has repeatedly come under attack in recent weeks.According to officials, this was the fourth attack on travellers along the same highway since last month. Insurgents have repeatedly targeted people travelling through the area despite a major security operation carried out following the earlier incidents.Security forces have now sealed off the area and launched a search operation to locate those responsible for the latest attack.The incident adds to the continuing security challenges in Balochistan, where armed insurgent groups have carried out attacks against security forces and civilians.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Both sides interested’: Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman’s first India visit likely in August 20-25 window
articles.summary: South Asia News: Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is likely to undertake his first official visit to India in the August 20-25 window, with the two capitals cu.
articles.body: Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is likely to undertake his first official visit to India in the August 20-25 window, with the two capitals currently discussing the exact dates.“Both sides have been interested in a bilateral visit, but the schedule was an issue. After weighing various schedules, the top officials of both countries have come close to a schedule between August 20 and 25,” Bangladesh’s The Daily Star quoted a diplomatic source in New Delhi as saying.As per the report, two possible schedules are currently under consideration — August 20-21 and August 21-22.The final dates are expected to be decided after Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi resumes his duties in Dhaka.The development comes after Trivedi held a one-on-one meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on August 11, a day after meeting Rahman in Dhaka.The proposed visit assumes significance amid recent diplomatic tensions between Bangladesh and India following deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s public remarks from New Delhi, where she has been living since being ousted after a student-led uprising on August 5, 2024. It was her first interaction with the press since her ouster.Dhaka had objected to Sheikh Hasina’s interaction, which was held on the second anniversary of her government’s ouster. In response, New Delhi pointed out that it was a private event and that India would not endorse her remarks.On Monday, during the meeting between Rahman and Trivedi, Bangladesh expressed “hope” that India would expedite the extradition process for the former prime minister.According to a statement issued by the Bangladesh Prime Minister’s Office, “Bangladesh expressed hope that India will expedite the extradition process of Sheikh Hasina.”Rahman became prime minister after his Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) swept the parliamentary elections in February. The BNP government succeeded the caretaker administration led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, which governed the country following Hasina’s ouster.Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home by December.(With ANI inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bangladesh PM's proposed India visit conditional on Hasina extradition, officials say
articles.summary: South Asia News: Bangladesh has said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s proposed visit to India will depend on the extradition of former premier Sheikh Hasina.Bangladesh’.
articles.body: Bangladesh has said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s proposed visit to India will depend on the extradition of former premier Sheikh Hasina.Bangladesh’s foreign ministry said on Sunday that Dhaka had urged New Delhi to accelerate the process of extraditing Hasina and other fugitives. The comments came as speculation grew over whether Rahman would travel to India later this month for his first official visit since becoming prime minister.Foreign ministry official A.K.M. Shahidul Karim played down reports that Rahman was certain to travel to India next week, saying that the necessary conditions for such a visit had yet to be established.“We are of the view that a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit,” Karim told reporters.He added that Bangladesh had asked Indian authorities to “expedite their efforts to extradite Sheikh Hasina and other fugitives.”India has previously said Bangladesh’s request for Hasina’s extradition is “under examination.”The development comes as the two governments have been discussing a possible visit by Rahman, with August 20-25 emerging as a potential window. Reports have suggested that officials were considering dates around August 20-21 or August 21-22, although the visit has not been formally confirmed.The proposed trip would carry particular significance given the strained state of India-Bangladesh relations since Hasina was forced from power during a student-led uprising in August 2024 and subsequently moved to India. She remains in India and faces a death sentence in Bangladesh after being convicted of crimes against humanity.Hasina has continued to make public statements from India, something Dhaka has objected to. Karim said her recent media interactions had further complicated the atmosphere surrounding Rahman’s proposed visit.The issue of Hasina's extradition has already featured in recent diplomatic contacts. During a meeting between Rahman and Indian high commissioner Dinesh Trivedi, Bangladesh expressed hope that India would speed up the extradition process, according to the Bangladesh prime minister's office.At the same time, India and Bangladesh have been exploring a broader reset in bilateral ties. Issues likely to feature in discussions include border management, trade, visa normalisation and water-sharing, while India is expected to raise security concerns, minority protection and Dhaka's growing ties with China and Pakistan.Rahman has already travelled to Malaysia and China since taking office but has not yet made the traditional first overseas visit to India.His government has also signalled a “Bangladesh First” foreign policy focused on sovereignty and non-interference, while saying it wants mutually beneficial relations with India and other countries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: From hospitals to schools: China expands scrutiny of religious beliefs in Chengdu
articles.summary: China News: China has expanded scrutiny of religious affiliation into public workplaces and schools in Chengdu. Employees at a public hospital were ordered to dis.
articles.body: China has expanded scrutiny of religious affiliation into public workplaces and schools in Chengdu. Employees at a public hospital were ordered to disclose their religious beliefs and education authorities collected information on the religious backgrounds of students and their families, according to The Epoch Times.The report, published on August 14, is based on leaked internal documents and accounts from people familiar with the practices who spoke anonymously, citing concerns about possible reprisals.An internal notice circulated by a public hospital in Chengdu said it was conducting a comprehensive survey of employees' religious beliefs as part of its "regular investigation of ideological, ethnic, and religious work."The notice said the survey was to cover every employee, including permanent staff, contracted workers and temporary workers.Employees were instructed to provide information about their religious affiliation and not conceal or omit relevant details. Those with no religious affiliation were also required to register as having "no religious belief", according to the report.The notice further said members of the Chinese Communist Party are not permitted to practise a religion and that employees with religious affiliations were required to report the matter to their Party branch.Religious activities and proselytising were also prohibited in the workplace, according to the document.An administrative employee at a university in Sichuan told The Epoch Times that schools were also investigating the religious affiliations of students' family members and compiling the information for submission to higher authorities.An employee at Chengdu's education authorities separately told the outlet that schools conduct background checks on students' families every year before new students enter school, with religious affiliation among the information collected.The report said the information collected by schools is passed up the administrative chain, although one source said they did not know how it was ultimately used.The reported measures form part of a wider Chinese Communist Party approach that treats religious affairs as an issue of political and ideological management, according to The Epoch Times.The Chinese government has promoted a policy known as the "Sinicisation of religion", under which religious groups are expected to align their activities with Chinese law and the political and cultural priorities of the state.Chinese president Xi Jinping has also called for stronger Party leadership over religious affairs and for religious work to be incorporated into the Party's broader leadership system, according to the report.A Chinese scholar cited by The Epoch Times said similar restrictions on religious belief among public employees exist in other parts of the country, but those claims were not independently verified in the report.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An 18-year-old construction worker in Belgium uncovered a €9 million gold hoard hidden inside a former brewery cellar
articles.summary: Europe News: An 18-year-old named Kobe was spending his summer break working construction in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, a small community in East Flanders, Belgium, .
articles.body: An 18-year-old named Kobe was spending his summer break working construction in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, a small community in East Flanders, Belgium, when an ordinary day of demolition work turned into the find of a lifetime. His crew had been renovating a former brewery building, once the home of a brewer in the early 20th century, and needed to remove part of the foundation in the cellar to lay a new sewer pipe. As they dug, Kobe noticed something unusual lying in the debris. What initially looked like ordinary €1 coins turned out to be part of a hoard containing gold coins, nuggets and bars that had been deliberately sealed inside a bricked-in section of the cellar wall, undisturbed for an unknown period until the construction work exposed it. The discovery was eventually estimated at roughly €9 million, transforming a routine summer job into one of Belgium's most extraordinary recent treasure finds. The hidden cache may have remained undiscovered for decades, preserved behind masonry through wars, ownership changes and repeated renovations until its accidental exposure at last.What construction workers found sealed inside the Belgian cellar wallKobe initially thought some of the metal pieces scattered in the rubble were loose euro coins. It was Kobe himself who then spotted a gold nugget lying among the debris, the moment that made clear the discovery was something far more valuable. According to a statement reported by VRT NWS, Belgium's public broadcaster, local police in Dendermonde confirmed that the discovery included numbered gold ingots and old gold pounds, deliberately hidden inside the wall rather than simply lost at the site. Site manager Mario described his reaction after his crew began shouting that they had found gold, saying he went to inspect the discovery and watched as more coins and bars emerged from the wall. The hoard has been estimated at roughly 40 gold bars and 4,000 coins.Why Belgian police moved quickly to secure the site and the goldOnce the crew realised the scale of what they had found, they contacted their employer, who instructed them to notify both the client and police. Officers from the local Dendermonde police force arrived and documented the discovery before the gold was transferred to a secure government facility. Authorities are investigating the hoard, including its origin and who may have a legal claim to it. Police also urged members of the public to stay away from the site after news of the discovery spread, and people began arriving in search of additional treasure, warning that the building remained an active construction site with exposed pits and machinery. The total value of the hoard has been estimated at approximately €9 million.What happens next for the gold and the workers who found itThe ownership of the gold has not yet been settled. Belgian law distinguishes between an ordinary lost or found object, for which an original owner can potentially reclaim the item within a five-year period, and a treasure, legally defined as an object hidden or buried for which no one can establish ownership. Under Article 716 of the Belgian Civil Code, if a treasure is found on someone else's property, it belongs half to the person who discovers it and half to the owner of the property. That means the eventual division of this particular hoard cannot yet be stated with certainty until authorities establish how the gold is legally classified and whether its original owner or their successors can still be identified.CAW Oost-Vlaanderen owns the building, and the organisation has said that if it ultimately receives proceeds from the discovery, it would use them to create additional shelter capacity for homeless people in the province. For Kobe, who was the person who first spotted the gold nugget, the immediate hope is that he will receive some form of finder's reward or share if the legal process ultimately recognises his claim. Authorities are still investigating where the gold came from, when it was hidden and who, if anyone, legally owns it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Needs to be moved to hospital now': Imran Khan's health in jail deteriorates
articles.summary: Pakistan News: NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan President Arif Alvi on Tuesday raised the alarm over jailed ex-PM Imran Khan’s worsening health, saying his medical reports.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan President Arif Alvi on Tuesday raised the alarm over jailed ex-PM Imran Khan’s worsening health, saying his medical reports were “alarming” and pointing to anxiety, heart palpitations and high blood pressure.In a post on X, Alvi said, "Imran Khan's medical reports are alarming. I have gone through them with several specialists, and I am writing this in plain language so every Pakistani can understand exactly what is happening."Alvi said the issues that concerned him most were Khan's "anxiety and stress levels", "palpitations," and "high blood pressure." He added that while sleeplessness was not mentioned in the report, Khan's medication appeared to suggest the problem."I have known Imran Khan for more than 35 years. Stress was never his weakness. That it is now at peak levels tells you everything about what three years of imprisonment and total isolation have done to him," he said.Alvi attributed Khan's stress to the political situation in Pakistan, the imprisonment and deaths of his colleagues, his own prolonged isolation and limited access to newspapers, books and information from outside.He also raised concerns over former PM and the only world-cup winning cricket captain Imran Khan's heart rate, which he said had increased to 54 beats per minute (bpm), compared with his historically lower resting rate."His heart rate is 54 bpm. Doctors will call that 'normal.' It is not normal for him," Alvi said, adding that Khan had also reported heart palpitations.Alvi called for Khan to undergo immediate cardiac monitoring, saying he "needs a 24-hour Holter monitor immediately". He also urged regular monitoring of his blood pressure.He recommended several tests, including a stress test, echocardiogram, cardiac MRI, cardiac artery calcium scan and cardiac CT angiogram, along with any other tests doctors may consider necessary."I am deeply worried. Isolation is taking a physical toll on his body. If this is not addressed immediately, the damage may become irreversible with more complications to follow," Alvi said.Calling for Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf founder Khan to be shifted to a hospital, Alvi said, "Imran Khan definitely needs to be moved to a hospital environment now, under an independent panel of doctors.""Neither his family nor the people of Pakistan trust government-appointed doctors alone," he added."The next three months will decide whether his condition is reversed or becomes permanent," Alvi said. He further said, "We all are alarmed. The country needs him more than ever before."Khan remains behind bars, while his sons, Sulaiman Khan and Kasim Khan, have also raised concerns about their father's access to his family, lawyers and doctors."We have no updates because his family, doctors and lawyers haven't been allowed to see him for seven months," they told CNN earlier this month.The statements came amid nationwide demonstrations by supporters of Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), who have demanded the release of the former prime minister and his wife, Bushra Bibi.Khan served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 until his ouster through a parliamentary no-confidence vote in 2022. He has been imprisoned since 2023 following convictions in several cases, including graft charges and the alleged disclosure of official secrets.Khan and his political aides have consistently alleged that the cases against him are politically motivated and intended to prevent his return to politics.After his ouster, Khan led nationwide rallies alleging that the government of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had conspired with Pakistan's military establishment and Washington to remove him. The subsequent crackdown targeted PTI leaders and supporters, while the party was barred from contesting the 2024 general elections.Khan's supporters have repeatedly maintained that the legal proceedings against him are politically motivated and aimed at blocking his political comeback.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1986, a rancher saw hundreds of wild horses crammed into a government feedlot: Two years later, he created an 11,000-acre refuge
articles.summary: US News: Rancher and author Dayton O. Hyde saw hundreds of wild horses in a Bureau of Land Management feedlot in Nevada in 1986. The animals had been removed f.
articles.body: Rancher and author Dayton O. Hyde saw hundreds of wild horses in a Bureau of Land Management feedlot in Nevada in 1986. The animals had been removed from public rangelands and were among horses the federal adoption program had not placed in private homes. Hyde's response was to imagine a large tract of land where unwanted mustangs could live in herds rather than remain in holding facilities. Two years later, that idea became the Black Hills Wild Horse Sanctuary in southwestern South Dakota, and covered 11,000 acres.The account of Hyde's 1986 visit appears in a report by South Dakota Public Broadcasting, which says the sight of the horses in the Nevada feedlot gave him the idea for a sanctuary. The report also states that Hyde founded the Institute of Range and the American Mustang in 1988 and secured land along the Cheyenne River, between Hot Springs and Edgemont, with help from then-Gov. George Mickelson.Hyde's plan emerged from a broader problem involving the management of wild horses in the American West. Congress had passed the Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act in 1971, placing responsibility for managing and protecting these animals on federal agencies. The Bureau of Land Management says it must also remove excess animals from public lands when herd numbers threaten the ecological balance of the range. Horses removed from the range can enter adoption and other placement programs, while animals that are not placed may remain in off-range care.The idea took shape in South DakotaThe Black Hills Wild Horse Sanctuary's account says Hyde traveled to Washington after seeing the horses and petitioned Congress about his proposal. South Dakota Gov. George Mickelson later invited him to inspect a tract of land known as Chilson Canyon in the southern Black Hills. A partnership eventually involved Hyde, the state, the Bureau of Land Management and the South Dakota Community Foundation.The sanctuary's records describe the project as requiring extensive preparation before the horses could arrive. Fences had to be built across the property, which consisted of rough range country rather than a ready-made horse facility. In the early fall of 1988, the first truckload of mustangs reached the sanctuary. One of the horses in that first group was a two-year-old blue roan filly named Prairie Lark, according to the organization's history.A refuge for horses that were not adoptedThe sanctuary was not established as another federal holding facility; it was designed as a private nonprofit refuge where groups of horses could live within the boundaries of the property. SDPB reported that the Institute of Range and the American Mustang owned the 11,000-acre sanctuary and that it housed mustangs the BLM adoption program had not placed, including older or injured animals.The BLM's modern Wild Horse and Burro Program uses adoption, sales, transfers and off-range facilities as part of its management system. The agency says its responsibility includes managing herd populations and removing excess animals when necessary to protect the health of public rangelands. Since 1971, it has placed hundreds of thousands of wild horses and burros into private care through adoption and other programs. Hyde's project addressed one part of that larger challenge. Instead of focusing on training a horse for an individual adopter, the sanctuary provided land where groups of mustangs could remain together. The site also protected a large section of private range in the Black Hills from other forms of development.The sanctuary continued after Hyde's deathHyde had worked as a rancher and written numerous books before founding the sanctuary, and remained closely associated with the project for the rest of his life. He died in December 2018, and the sanctuary has continued under the nonprofit organization created around his original project. Its current mission still centers on maintaining the land as habitat while providing a home for unwanted wild horses. The property is located near Hot Springs in southwestern South Dakota, where mustang herds continue to roam within the sanctuary's boundaries.The strongest verified fact in Hyde's story remains the sequence that began with the Nevada feedlot. He saw a large number of wild horses that had nowhere to go through the adoption system, developed the idea of a refuge, and by 1988 had established an 11,000-acre sanctuary in South Dakota. More than three decades later, the land remains dedicated to wild horses and the surrounding habitat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Middle East News: The United Arab Emirates’ defence ministry said on Tuesday that it had detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran towards the Gulf country, as.
articles.body: The United Arab Emirates’ defence ministry said on Tuesday that it had detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran towards the Gulf country, as tensions continued to rise across the region.The ministry said both missiles fell into water, with one landing outside the UAE’s territorial waters and the other inside them. It said the country remained prepared to respond to any threats.“The Ministry of Defence confirms that it is on high alert and fully prepared to deal with any threats, and to firmly confront anything aimed at undermining the security of the state, thereby ensuring the preservation of its sovereignty, security and stability, and protecting its interests and national capabilities,” it added.The ministry said that it is 'ready to deal with any threats.'The missile launches came as efforts continued to reach an agreement between Iran and Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global shipping. US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the US had no talks planned with Iran, while insisting the strait remained “open and operating” despite sharply reduced traffic.Trump also said the US blockade of Iranian ports remained “in full force and effect” and claimed that all water mines had been removed. He posted a map depicting the Strait of Hormuz as US territory.Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded on X, saying: “Just as Trump correctly wrote the name of the eternal Persian Gulf, soon his delusion regarding the Strait of Hormuz will either be corrected or we will correct the delusions of this deluded man," he wrote on X.Shipping data platform Kpler said confirmed crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell 19.5% last week to 95, with only three vessels passing through on Sunday. No vessels used the Omani routes.Meanwhile, an unidentified projectile damaged the engine room of a ship near Oman, causing “a crew casualty”, according to the British military’s UK Maritime Trade Operations centre. The Omani Coast Guard was assisting the crew, while authorities investigated.Separately, Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed they had launched drones at an oil refinery operated by Saudi Aramco in Saudi Arabia. There were no immediate reports of damage.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: How to open a coconut without a hammer: 5 easy methods to crack the shell at home
articles.summary: A whole coconut can seem almost impossible to open without brute force. Its shell is hard and thick. The fruit inside is soft and full of water. Yet t.
articles.body: A whole coconut can seem almost impossible to open without brute force. Its shell is hard and thick. The fruit inside is soft and full of water. Yet there is no need for a hammer to get through it. A few everyday tools and the right technique can do this task easily. A rolling pin can weaken the shell. An oven can make the shell easier to separate from the flesh. Even a sturdy outdoor surface can help when used with care. The key is not to hit harder but to work around the shell. Before beginning, the coconut water should be drained through one of its three eyes. The coconut should then be placed on a stable surface before opening it. Here are five simple ways to open a coconut without a hammer. With patience and the right approach, anyone can crack open a fresh coconut safely at home, avoiding the mess and risk that come with forceful hammering. Each method works by creating small weaknesses in the tough outer shell rather than relying on a single powerful blow. Choosing the best technique depends on the tools available, the coconut’s size, and how much control you want.5 simple ways to open a coconut without a hammer using everyday household tools1. Use a heavy rolling pinStart by draining the coconut water. Then place the coconut on a folded kitchen towel so it does not roll across the area. Use a heavy rolling pin to tap the shell around and rotate the coconut. The aim is to weaken the shell along one line rather than smash one spot repeatedly.After several rounds of tapping, a crack should begin to appear. Keep working around the shell until the crack becomes longer and deeper. Once the coconut starts to split, stop striking it. Pull the pieces apart carefully.A solid wooden or metal rolling pin works better than a lightweight one. Do not use excessive force, as the coconut can shift suddenly, and the rolling pin can slip. Once the shell is open, use a sturdy spoon to loosen the white flesh from the inside.2. Use the blunt side of a sturdy knifeA sturdy kitchen knife can help crack a coconut, but the safest approach is to use its blunt side. Do not try to stab the shell with the blade.Drain the coconut and place it on a stable chopping board. Hold it firmly with one hand while keeping fingers away from the area being struck. Use the blunt back of the knife to tap around the shell's middle. The shell should gradually develop a crack. Once that happens, put the knife aside and open the coconut by hand.This method needs more care than a rolling pin. A knife can slip if too much force is used. If the coconut keeps moving or the shell does not respond to gentle tapping, switch to another method.3. Use oven heatHeat can make the shell easier to separate from the coconut flesh. Start by draining all the coconut water through one of its three eyes. Place the whole coconut on a baking tray and heat it in an oven for 10 to 15 minutes. Keep an eye on it while it heats. The shell may begin to develop cracks. Use oven gloves when removing the tray.Let the coconut cool until it is safe to handle. You can then tap it gently against a sturdy surface or use a blunt utensil to help separate the cracked shell. The heat may also make the white flesh easier to remove. Do not place a coconut containing liquid in the oven. Heating a sealed coconut can allow pressure to build inside. Draining it first is an important safety step.4. Use a hard outdoor surfaceSometimes gravity can do what a hammer cannot. Drain the coconut first. Wrap it in a thick kitchen towel or place it inside a strong bag. This helps contain broken shell pieces. Drop it from a low height onto the hard surface.Check the coconut after each attempt. Once a crack appears, open the coconut carefully. Collect the broken pieces before removing the flesh. Do not throw the coconut or drop it from a great height. A controlled drop is enough to test the shell.This method is best treated as a last resort. If the coconut does not crack easily, use a more controlled technique instead of increasing the height.5. Tap the coconut against a sturdy stone or doorstepA solid, blunt surface can create the same kind of repeated impact as a hammer. Drain the coconut and wrap it in a thick towel first. Hold the towel-covered coconut firmly. Tap one section against a sturdy stone, concrete doorstep, or another surface that can withstand the impact. Rotate the coconut after each tap.The shell should gradually weaken until a crack appears. Avoid glass, delicate tiles, and fragile tops. They can break under heavy impact. An outdoor concrete surface is a better choice.Once the coconut cracks, place it on a stable surface. Separate the pieces carefully and watch for sharp shell edges. This method provides more control than simply throwing the coconut.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: An unstable rock formation threatens the existence of an entire Swiss village of 1,300 residents as thawing glaciers destabilise the Alps
articles.summary: Europe News: The Swiss village of Kandersteg could be destroyed by a landslide due to an unstable mountain rock formation, and scientists are linking the threat to.
articles.body: The Swiss village of Kandersteg could be destroyed by a landslide due to an unstable mountain rock formation, and scientists are linking the threat to thawing permafrost and glacier dynamics. The 1,300 residents of the village in Switzerland's Bern canton live in the midst of a charming landscape including sharp peaks, white glaciers, steep green valleys and it is this natural surrounding that could take it over, as per a report by CNN.A mountainside rock formation called Spitze Stei, part of a mountain landscape increasingly affected by thawing permafrost, threatens to collapse the valley in a massive landslide. There has been a heightened threat of rockslides in Kandersteg since 2018, when paragliders noted that the rock formation was losing height and that pieces had broken off it, according to a Reuters report. “You are aware that it’s happening, but not afraid,” said Brigitte Jüni, an inhabitant of Kandersteg, to the CNN. She said authorities took all the precautions they could. “But then it’s nature. It’s nature, and you never know,” Jüni added.Thawing permafrostAs glaciers permafrost thaw, the frozen soil sediment and rock that bind and hold mountains together melt due to higher temperatures caused by climate change, ultimately increasing the threat of landslides in the Swiss Alps. In May 2025, a huge mass of rock and ice from a glacier thundered down the mountainside in the nearby Loetschental valley, sending plumes of dust skyward and coating all of Blatten, a village with 300 residents, with mud. This village had been evacuated earlier as a precaution. Blatten was evacuated 10 days before the deluge, which caused insurance losses of 320 million Swiss francs ($400 million), an initial estimate by the Swiss insurance association showed.For Kandersteg, the threat is not immediate and thus people have not yet been evacuated. However, there are plans in place for an evacuation if necessary. The village's dams and daily monitoring with researchers checking the mountain via GPS, radar and drone have it prepared to avert a disaster. In the event of major rock movement, residents should receive warnings at least 48 hours in advance.“This isn’t the same case as in Blatten. It’s a different situation,” said local resident Rudolf Isler. “We are not afraid of the Spitze Stei rock. It’s been many years seeing stones falling from up there. The problem here is about global warming and rising temperatures.”Kandersteg was a prime example of an area with historical structural instability that could be aggravated by many factors, including permafrost, said Robert Kenner at the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research in Davos. "What calmed down for about 3,000 years is now reactivated," he said. Sensors monitoring GPS locations on the Spitzer Stein showed the mountain shifting by up to 70 centimetres (2.3 feet) a day, said Kandersteg's mayor Rene Maeder.Just the beginningKandersteg has spent over 11 million Swiss francs ($13.81 million) on disaster preparedness, including dams to slow down flooding, said the mayor. Residents, who get regular updates on the mountain's movements via email and WhatsApp, have faith in the technology. "We still sleep well," said Patrick Jost, head of Kandersteg's tourism office, whose home is one of the most exposed to a potential Spitzer Stein collapse to Reuters.Markus Stoffel, professor for climate change and natural risks at the University of Geneva said climate change leads to the melting of both glaciers and permafrost. “In the mountains and in the unconsolidated debris, there is lots of ice,” Stoffel said. “Once this ice is melting, it acts like a cement. These mountain slopes will become increasingly unstable.”If the entire unstable section of the Spitze Stei, estimated at roughly 15 to 20 million cubic meters were to collapse, it would trigger a massive natural disaster. But the rock is under consistent monitoring, evacuation plans have been prepared and experts are of the opinion that it is more likely to break down gradually than in one huge chunk.Nathan Solothurnmann, a climate and energy expert for Greenpeace Switzerland, says that climate change means landslides or avalanches will become more common.“Maybe even one day we will have to abandon certain valleys or certain villages because it’s becoming impossible to live there,” Solothurnmann said. “Or the measure you will need to take to protect infrastructure is so expensive, the efforts are so big, that it’s not worthwhile anymore living there.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Queen Camilla says she nearly revealed King Charles III’s cancer diagnosis days before palace announcement
articles.summary: Europe News: Queen Camilla has shared for the first time her struggle to keep King Charles III’s cancer diagnosis private.This revelation came during a visit to a .
articles.body: Queen Camilla has shared for the first time her struggle to keep King Charles III’s cancer diagnosis private.This revelation came during a visit to a cancer support center just five days before Buckingham Palace officially announced the diagnosis. On January 31, 2024, Camilla opened a new Maggie’s center at the Royal Free Hospital in London.At that time, Charles had already received his cancer diagnosis, which had not yet been made public, although it was known that he was recovering from treatment for an enlarged prostate. Buckingham Palace announced the cancer diagnosis on February 5.Camilla, who is president of Maggie’s, said knowing about her husband’s diagnosis changed the way she spoke to cancer patients and their families during the visit. “I remember coming to see a Maggie’s just after the king being diagnosed. Nobody could say anything at the time. That was quite difficult,” she said.The remarks appear in a seven-minute anniversary film posted on Wednesday to the Royal Family and Maggie’s YouTube channels. Camilla was filmed speaking with Maggie’s chief executive Dame Laura Lee at Clarence House, news agency The Guardian reported.'I almost said something’, says Queen CamillaLooking back at her January 2024 visit, Camilla said: “I almost said something but, you know, I felt that it wasn’t the time to say.”“[I] looked at everybody who was suffering and all the relations and I think it made me realise even more how important these places were.”She told Lee: “I was just longing to let it out but obviously I couldn’t.”Camilla said her conversations with people at the centre also felt different because of what she knew about Charles. She found herself “almost questioning them”, but said she did not “want to pry too deeply”.“But normally when I went in, I was just talking to them, but I don’t know, I felt it was much more deep,” she said.Buckingham Palace said on February 5, 2024, that a separate issue of concern had been detected while Charles was being treated for benign prostate enlargement. Further tests identified a form of cancer, though the palace did not disclose which type. Charles began regular treatment and put public-facing engagements on hold while continuing state business and official paperwork.Camilla says diagnosis changed life at homeCamilla said her experience of meeting people affected by cancer took on a different meaning once the illness directly affected her family.“It had never really come back to roost at home, and suddenly your husband is diagnosed, and you think ‘Goodness I’ve been talking to all these people and now I’m the one with some relation, who’s got to help to look after my poor husband and try and understand it all.’”She became president of Maggie’s in 2008 and has visited 18 of its 27 UK centres, many more than once. The charity opened its first centre in Edinburgh in 1996.Charles resumed public-facing duties on April 30, 2024, less than three months after treatment began, visiting the University College Hospital Macmillan Cancer Centre in London with Camilla. Speaking about his determination to continue working, Camilla said: “Look at my husband. Nothing stopped him. He just said, ‘This is my way. I’m going to cope with it.’”In December 2025, Charles said early diagnosis and effective intervention meant his cancer-treatment schedule could be reduced in 2026.Maggie’s aims for 60 UK centresCamilla also used the film to draw attention to Maggie’s work with families and its efforts to encourage more men affected by cancer to seek support.Maggie’s offers free psychological, emotional and practical help without requiring an appointment or referral. Its 27 centres operate alongside major NHS cancer hospitals across the UK and help hundreds of thousands of people annually.Camilla said every hospital should have a Maggie’s centre. Maggie’s aims to have a centre at all 60 major cancer hospitals in the UK.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Message to Europe - it can receive missiles': Iran warns of wider war if Trump attacks, says report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran has considered targeting US military assets in Europe if US President Donald Trump escalates the ongoing war, according to  regime insiders cited.
articles.body: Iran has considered targeting US military assets in Europe if US President Donald Trump escalates the ongoing war, according to regime insiders cited by the Financial Times.Two people close to the Iranian regime said Iranian forces had examined targets in countries such as Bulgaria, which recently approved the use of its Bezmer air base for US refuelling aircraft.Cyprus was also being considered as a potential target, one insider added. A British air base there was also hit by a drone in March.Iranian forces have separately examined the possibility of attacking undersea fibre-optic cables in the Strait of Hormuz if the conflict escalates further, according to the insiders.The threats reflect a growing conviction inside Iran's ruling circles that a return to full-scale war is inevitable. Negotiations over the strait remain stalled, and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has recently elevated hardliners to key security and military posts, signalling a hardening of Tehran's stance. Trump said on Tuesday that "no talks or conversations" were underway with Iran.The IRGC has already warned that "any base used to launch an attack on Iranian territory will be considered a legitimate target," a direct reference to UK bases used by the US.One regime insider told the FT that Iran was preparing to widen the conflict if Trump followed through on previous threats to attack Iranian infrastructure. The second said Tehran would place “no limits” on its response if the US launched an attack."If the US goes too far, Iran will defend itself at any price — beyond the region and into Europe," the second insider said.Iran has already demonstrated its willingness to target locations far from the Middle East.In February, the US accused Tehran of firing several missiles towards Diego Garcia, a joint US-UK military base in the Indian Ocean, although none reached their target. Turkey also said in March that its Nato air defences intercepted several ballistic missiles launched from Iran.The UK’s Akrotiri air base in Cyprus was also struck by a drone in March.Western officials at the time suspected the drone had been launched by Iranian proxy forces rather than directly by Tehran.The insiders also pointed to an Iranian attack on a US base in Jordan last month that killed three American service members as evidence of Tehran's improving long-range strike capabilities.“This was also a message to Europe: it can receive missiles, so it should know where it should stand in this war,” one insider said, warning that a major US attack on Iranian infrastructure could push the conflict beyond the region.However, analysts cautioned that Iran's ability to strike Europe remains limited.Sidharth Kaushal, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute told FT that the threat posed by Iranian missiles to targets in Europe and elsewhere as "real, but limited." Iran could deploy medium-range ballistic missiles against US assets in southern and southeastern Europe, such as its Shahab series, but Kaushal said these would struggle to do damage at longer ranges.Analysts also said Iran could rely more heavily on regional proxies, including Shia militias in Iraq, Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen, rather than relying solely on long-range missile attacks.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Mexican couple bought a failed coconut farm 30 years ago; the 346-acre wasteland is now a wildlife haven for turtles, dolphins and flamingos
articles.summary: Three decades ago, a 346-acre stretch of land on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula was little more than the remains of a failed coconut farm.
articles.body: Three decades ago, a 346-acre stretch of land on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula was little more than the remains of a failed coconut farm. Disease had swept through millions of palms across the region, leaving behind a stripped and barren landscape. Mónica Hernández and her husband, architect and painter Aníbal González, saw something different in the neglected property they bought at El Cuyo. They had noticed the flamingos and spoonbills living nearby and decided to let the landscape recover rather than rebuild the plantation that had been lost. Over the years, native vegetation returned and the coastal estate became a haven for wildlife, with sea turtles, dolphins and flamingos now part of its surroundings. The couple also developed plans for an eco-conscious luxury residential complex; after 30 years, they are putting the £87 million estate on the market while keeping a small piece for themselves. Their decades-long commitment shows how patient, thoughtful stewardship can turn a damaged landscape into a thriving sanctuary for both wildlife and future generations.Their approach gradually transformed the property from a damaged agricultural site into a diverse coastal landscape, showing how natural recovery can reshape land over generations. Today, the estate combines conservation, architecture and luxury, reflecting the couple’s long-term vision for the remote peninsula. How coconut disease devastated the Yucatán Peninsula and transformed El CuyoThe condition of the property was tied to a wider problem affecting the Yucatán Peninsula. Millions of coconut palms had been damaged by an aggressive plant disease in the 1990s, leaving areas that had once been productive looking almost empty. El Cuyo was among the places where the effects were visible, but Hernández and González did not see the damaged landscape simply as a failed agricultural site. They were drawn to the wildlife around it, particularly the flamingos and spoonbills they encountered in the area.The couple put what Hernández described as “big money” into the secluded property around 30 years ago. Rather than trying to recreate the old coconut plantation, they allowed the landscape to change. Once the dead coconut trees were burnt, the original vegetation began returning, according to Hernández. That regeneration became part of what the couple were trying to preserve. The result was a private coastal estate where the surrounding natural environment became as important as the buildings and other improvements made to the land. Whoever eventually acquires El Cuyo will inherit not just a luxury property, but also the responsibility of safeguarding this extraordinary ecological achievement.How El Cuyo became a wildlife haven for flamingos, turtles and dolphinThe property now stretches across more than 346 acres, with roughly four miles of beachfront. Its setting on the northern Yucatán Peninsula puts it alongside a coastline already known for its wildlife, and the estate has become a place where animals are a regular part of the landscape rather than an attraction brought in for visitors. Flamingos and spoonbills were among the species that first caught the couple’s attention, while turtles and dolphins later became familiar sights around the property.Hernández told The Sun that dolphins arrive during certain seasons, describing their appearance as something unusual and beautiful. The couple also said they regularly spend time at the estate and enjoy seeing turtles and dolphins along the coast. The surrounding waters have helped shape the experience of El Cuyo, with wealthy visitors sometimes arriving by yacht and swimming towards the white beaches.How the 346-acre El Cuyo property could become a luxury eco-resortThe estate has since moved beyond being a private coastal retreat. Hernández and González received approval from the Mexican government for a residential development at El Cuyo, with the condition that the project follows ecological conservation requirements. Working with Casa e Progetti, they produced plans for a resort using renewable energy and natural resources rather than treating the surrounding environment as an afterthought.The proposed scheme includes 64 villas, each planned on plots ranging from 2.5 to 6.9 acres, with a section of private beachfront. The homes would average about 5,000 square feet and contain four or five bedrooms. Their design is intended to draw on Mayan architectural influences, with oval forms, open-air spaces, wooden structures and stone walls. The plans therefore combine a high-end residential development with an attempt to retain the character of the coastal setting.Why the owners are selling their £87 million estate in MexicoAfter three decades of developing the property, Hernández and González have decided that El Cuyo should pass to someone younger who can devote more time to the next stage of the project. According to The Sun, the estate is marketed by Beauchamp Estates and has an asking price of £87 million, which makes it the most expensive property in Mexican history. The couple do not intend to leave the place entirely, though. They plan to retain a smaller section at the edge of the estate for themselves.The decision is partly about time. Hernández is 75, and González is 81, and she said the project had previously demanded their attention “24/7”. They now want to spend more time at their own beach without having to manage the entire development. For Hernández, the future of the property is also tied to how its next owner treats the land. She said it would suit an ecologist and that whoever lives there should act as a guardian of nature.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: From Kargil's Op Safed Sagar to Bholari's Op Sindoor: How Indian Air Force grew in capability
articles.summary: News News: A recently released web series Operation Safed Sagar has reignited public interest in the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) role during the Kargil War. It capt.
articles.body: A recently released web series Operation Safed Sagar has reignited public interest in the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) role during the Kargil War. It captures the improvisation and courage of pilots who, in 1999, fought at altitudes above 15,000 feet with limited precision weapons and inadequate intelligence. The IAF was constrained by political orders not to cross the Line of Control, forcing crews to invent high‑altitude strike profiles never practised before. Despite these limitations, the destruction of Pakistan’s logistics base at Muntho Dhalo proved decisive. Yet the campaign exposed gaps in joint planning, shortages of guided munitions and the obsolescence of many systems.Then 26 years later in May 2025, Operation Sindoor demonstrated this transformation. In response to the cold-blooded Pahalgam terror attack, the IAF and the army struck nine terror sites in Pakistan and Pakistan Occupied Kashmir. Pakistan escalated with drone, missile and air attacks, prompting India to retaliate. During the 88-hour conflict, The air force hit air-defence infrastructure at Lahore, Karachi, Sialkot, Chunian, Pasrur and Arifwala were degraded or destroyed, while airbases including Nur Khan (Chaklala), Rafiqui (Shorkot), Murid (Chakwal), Sargodha, Rahim Yar Khan, Sukkur, Shahbaz (Jacobabad) and Bholari bore the brunt of Brahmos, SCALP and Rampage strikes. Unlike Kargil, this was not improvisation but deliberate, proportionate aggression, executed with precision stand‑off weapons and detailed joint planning with sister services.This capability evolution can be best viewed in four separate verticals. These are equipment, the induction of aircraft such as the Rafales armed with SCALP and Hammer, Su‑30MKIs integrated with BrahMos and layered air defences which include S‑400, Akash and MRSAM gave the IAF credible defensive and offensive capacity. This is in contrast to the use of very limited use of precision guided bombs by the IAF in Kargil. The conflict is known for the innovations used by the air force in terms of both tactics and deployment of equipment.Training is another key factor, simulators, night operations and international exercises ensured crews were better prepared for the conflict. Jointness is the third leg of this table, with the Chief of Defence Staff and the three service chiefs downwards were involved in the planning and execution from the outset. Political resolve, the deliberations and directions at the political level in 1999, ensured that the armed forces do not cross the Line of Control, while during Op Sindoor and the Balakot air strikes the aim was to strike terror targets deep inside Pakistan.From Safed Sagar’s improvised high‑altitude bombing runs to Sindoor’s precision strikes on airbases and radar sites deep inside Pakistan, the IAF has evolved into a force capable of shaping outcomes at strategic depth. The contrast is stark: in 1999, limited stocks of laser‑guided bombs and political restrictions defined the campaign; in 2025, deliberate planning, advanced munitions and jointness delivered decisive results. The journey from Muntho Dhalo to Masroor reflects not just technological progress but a doctrinal renaissance, positioning Indian air power as a mature instrument of national strategy.

articles.title: Russia unleashes ballistic, cruise, hypersonic missiles and drones on Ukraine; Kyiv main target
articles.summary: Europe News: Russia launched a large overnight air assault on Ukraine, firing ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles and 168 drones, killing at least 12 people .
articles.body: Russia launched a large overnight air assault on Ukraine, firing ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles and 168 drones, killing at least 12 people and injuring more than 40 in Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukraine’s air force said on Thursday.The barrage damaged residential and public buildings, sparked fires and disrupted power supplies in parts of the capital, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, as Moscow intensified its aerial attacks on Ukraine.In Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district, a fire tore through a nine-storey residential building, destroying its upper floors and killing seven people, Klitschko said. He called for Friday to be observed as a day of mourning.“Two other districts also suffered damage,” Klitschko said on Telegram, with non-residential facilities, warehouses, a school and a children's hospital among those hit.Beyond the capital, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russian forces targeted gas infrastructure in northern Chernihiv and a border crossing with Moldova in the southern Odesa region.Quoting a witness, news agency Reuters reported hearing more than a dozen explosions in the Ukrainian capital. Ukraine’s emergency service released footage showing servicemen fighting fires and helping people escape damaged buildings.Power company DTEK said electricity had been restored to more than half of the roughly 90,000 homes that lost power in Kyiv following the attack.Zelenskiy described the assault as a major operation involving different types of weapons.“It was a massive attack – the Russians had been preparing for a long time, combining different types of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones, aiming to cause as much damage as possible to civilian infrastructure,” he said on X.A children’s hospital was struck in the Solomianskyi district to the west of the heart of the capital, with windows blown out and cars burned, according to the Guardian.Russia’s defence ministry said its forces struck facilities producing drone components, a military depot and a logistics hub in Kyiv and the surrounding region.The attack also had regional repercussions. Romania’s defence ministry said a drone crashed into its territory, while Moldova’s military said another drone crossed its airspace.Russia has intensified air attacks in recent months as Ukraine faces shortages of interceptors. Ukraine, meanwhile, has increased strikes on Russian oil facilities and logistics infrastructure.Diplomatic efforts have so far failed to secure a lasting ceasefire. Zelenskiy said Ukraine had submitted proposals to US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner for a plan to end the war, while Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow remained ready for talks at short notice.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2017, Germany’s Freiburg opened a city hall with solar-powered walls designed to produce more energy than the building needs
articles.summary: Europe News: In Freiburg, south-west Germany, a city hall has been designed to do something unusual for a government building: produce more energy than it consumes.
articles.body: In Freiburg, south-west Germany, a city hall has been designed to do something unusual for a government building: produce more energy than it consumes. Completed in 2017, the city’s latest town hall combines high-performance solar panels with an energy-efficient design that sharply reduces the building’s demand for heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting. The World Green Building Council lists City Hall Freiburg at Fehrenbachallee and describes it as a surplus-energy building, noting that photovoltaic units on the roof and sun-exposed parts of the façade generate more electricity than the building requires. The project goes beyond simply adding solar panels to an existing office. Its insulation, ventilation, heating and cooling systems were designed together as part of a wider energy concept. Freiburg’s official tourism site also notes that construction began in 2014 and that, after completion in 2017, the building was expected to generate more energy than it needed.Freiburg’s newest town hall was designed as an energy-producing buildingThe building is located at Fehrenbachallee in Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg, rather than at the historic Rathausplatz associated with Freiburg’s older town halls. The World Green Building Council identifies its construction/refurbishment date as 2017 and records its address as Fehrenbachallee, Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg 79106, Germany. That distinction is useful because Freiburg has several buildings referred to as town halls. The city’s official tourism website explains that the latest town hall was constructed between 2014 and 2017, while the older New Town Hall is a much earlier Renaissance complex. The modern building was therefore created specifically for contemporary administration, with energy performance incorporated into its architecture from the beginning. Rather than treating electricity generation as an addition, its designers made renewable energy and low consumption central to the building's operation.Solar panels cover the parts of the building exposed to sunlightOne of the most distinctive elements of the project is the way photovoltaic technology has been incorporated into both the roof and façade. The roof and areas of the façade exposed to direct sunlight are fitted with high-performance solar energy panels. These panels have a dual function: they generate electricity while also shielding parts of the building from direct solar radiation. That approach makes the building itself part of its energy infrastructure. Instead of requiring a separate solar farm or relying entirely on rooftop space, the architecture provides additional surfaces for electricity generation. The strategy is particularly relevant in urban areas, where land can be expensive and limited. Freiburg’s latest town hall demonstrates how walls and roofs that would normally serve only structural or protective purposes can also contribute to a building’s energy supply. The result is a structure where renewable-energy production is visible in the architecture rather than hidden away.Its insulation and ventilation systems help keep energy demand lowProducing large quantities of solar electricity is only half of the building’s energy strategy. Freiburg’s town hall was also designed to need less energy in the first place. The building has outstanding thermal insulation that permits low-temperature heating and high-temperature cooling. Its ventilation system incorporates heat recovery, reducing the amount of energy lost through the movement of indoor and outdoor air. The building also uses groundwater as part of its heating and cooling strategy. A heat pump operates the heating system, while a plate heat exchanger provides cooling. These systems work alongside the building envelope and ventilation system rather than functioning as isolated technologies. This integrated approach is important because an energy-positive building cannot depend solely on generating more electricity. Its performance also depends on controlling how much energy is required to maintain comfortable conditions for the people working inside.The building produces more electricity than it needsThe combination of low energy demand and substantial photovoltaic generation gives Freiburg’s town hall its defining characteristic. The World Green Building Council describes it as Europe’s biggest surplus-energy building and says its photovoltaic units produce more electricity than the building needs. The surplus does not simply disappear. The building can respond to requirements from the electricity network and feed excess electricity back into the grid. This means the town hall can function not only as an energy consumer but also as a small-scale producer contributing electricity beyond its own immediate needs. The concept changes the traditional relationship between buildings and power systems. Instead of a building continuously drawing electricity from an external network, the building can generate renewable power, satisfy its own requirements and return excess generation to the wider system.Freiburg turned everyday government architecture into a renewable-energy showcaseThe project is particularly striking because it applies advanced energy principles to an ordinary civic function. A city hall is primarily a workplace for public administration, yet Freiburg’s building has been designed to demonstrate what that workplace can achieve environmentally. The project is recorded under its net-zero operational carbon category and holds a DGNB Climate Positive certification. Freiburg's official tourism information places the project within the city's broader collection of town halls, but the 2017 building represents a sharp contrast with the historic structures. The older buildings reflect centuries of civic and architectural history; the latest one reflects a contemporary attempt to reduce the environmental cost of running a large public building. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the number of solar panels installed, but in how architecture, insulation, ventilation, heating, cooling and renewable generation were brought together into one energy concept.A city hall where the building can give electricity backFreiburg’s modern town hall demonstrates a different way of thinking about public buildings. Instead of designing a structure that simply consumes energy and then adding solar panels afterwards, the project combines low demand, renewable generation and energy-efficient systems from the outset. The building generates more energy than it requires for heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting, with surplus electricity capable of being fed into the grid. That makes the building more than an administrative workplace. Its roof and sun-facing façade generate power, its insulation reduces energy loss, its ventilation system recovers heat, and its heating and cooling systems make use of groundwater. Together, these features turn Freiburg’s town hall into a practical demonstration of how public architecture can contribute to the energy transition. Rather than merely occupying space within a city, the building actively produces some of the energy that the city and its occupants depend upon.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 83 members, 6 generations, one kitchen: Meet the extraordinary family from Andhra Pradesh where 50 kg of rice is cooked every day
articles.summary: At a time when joint families are becoming increasingly rare, one family in Andhra Pradesh is still living by the old idea of staying together literal.
articles.body: At a time when joint families are becoming increasingly rare, one family in Andhra Pradesh is still living by the old idea of staying together literally, in every sense. In Kurlapalli village of Anantapur district, 83 members of the Nagappa family, spread across six generations, live as one household. They occupy four adjoining houses, but share a kitchen, meals, finances, work and family decisions. And feeding this family is no small task. Around 50 kg of rice is cooked every day.As per PTI and various media, the Nagappa family is headed by elders Mutyalappa and Hanumantha Rayudu. The household includes six mothers-in-law, 14 daughters-in-law, 20 children, grandparents and other elderly members. Despite its size, the family follows a carefully organised routine that allows dozens of people to live, work and eat together.Every morning begins with a family meeting. The elders gather over coffee and decide what needs to be done that day, from the household menu and grocery purchases to farming work and other responsibilities. Members are assigned different tasks, with some heading to the fields while others stay back to cook and manage the home.“We divide work among the family members every morning,” Mutyalappa told BBC Telugu. “We ensure welfare, food, clothing and all other needs of the family.”One kitchen for 83 peopleThe family may live in four neighbouring houses, but there is no separate cooking for individual households. The food is prepared collectively, with the daughters-in-law working together in the kitchen and the elders overseeing purchases of groceries and other essentials.“Even now, no matter what we do, we make the same food for everyone,” Mahesh, one of the family’s sons, told BBC Telugu. “We make the same curry, rice, and porridge.”The scale of the cooking is difficult to imagine in an ordinary household. The family uses about 50 kg of rice a day, with large quantities of food prepared over firewood to feed everyone. The common kitchen is also part of the family's larger system of sharing. Income is pooled, expenses are shared and household needs are treated as collective responsibilities.Farming, buses and a shared incomeThe family's livelihood is built on more than agriculture. The Nagappas farm around 120 acres and also run a bus transport business. The family owns four buses operating between Kalyandurgam and parts of Karnataka.Income from farming and the transport business is managed collectively, helping support the large household. For the family, this arrangement is not simply about tradition. They believe staying together has played a major role in transforming their fortunes.Mutyalappa says the family came from extreme poverty. “We didn't have a blanket to cover ourselves, we only had one meal [a day] to eat. We have grown to this level now. This was possible only because we were all together. If we had been apart, we would never have reached this level.”“They do whatever I say”But the arrangement also reflects the traditional patriarchal structure of a large joint family. Hanumantha Rayudu, another senior member, says the responsibility of managing the family fell on him after the death of his father and grandfather.“Since the death of my father and grandfather, the burden of the family has fallen on me,” he told BBC Telugu. “We live by showing each one their own support. So far, we have not had any problems or differences. We have all worked hard together. They do whatever I say.”How 83 people make one home workThe Nagappa family is spread across four houses rather than literally sharing one building. But in practice, the boundaries between those homes appear to matter little. There is one common kitchen. There are common meals. Income is pooled. Household responsibilities are divided. Major decisions are discussed collectively.The elders plan the day, women manage the massive cooking operation, farming requires the labour of multiple family members and the transport business adds another source of income. articles.title: BNP leader Mirza Fakhrul Alamgir wins Bangladesh presidential election with 255 votes
articles.summary: South Asia News: Bangladesh has elected senior Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leader Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir as its 23rd president, marking a significant shift.
articles.body: Bangladesh has elected senior Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leader Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir as its 23rd president, marking a significant shift for a politician who until recently held one of the party's top organisational posts.Alamgir secured 255 votes in Thursday's presidential election held at the Jatiya Sangsad, Bangladesh's Parliament. His rival, Oli Ahmed, the candidate backed by an 11-party opposition alliance led by Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party (NCP), received 88 votes.The voting took place between 2 pm and 5 pm local time under the supervision of chief election commissioner AMM Nasir Uddin. Of the 349 MPs eligible to vote, 343 cast their ballots. The chief election commissioner later announced Alamgir as the winner.A contested presidential election after 35 yearsThursday's poll was notable because it was the first time in 35 years that more than one candidate contested Bangladesh's presidential election. The previous presidential election involving a parliamentary vote was held in 1991.Alamgir had been nominated as the BNP's presidential candidate last week. After receiving the nomination, he stepped down as BNP Secretary General and resigned from the party's National Standing Committee.BNP Senior Joint Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi announced his nomination following a meeting of the party's National Standing Committee near the Bangladesh Prime Minister's Office at the Secretariat. Rizvi said the decision followed discussions with Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman.Acting President and Speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad Hafiz Uddin Ahmed, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and other MPs also took part in Thursday's voting.Although the Jatiya Sangsad has 350 seats, only 349 members were eligible to vote because the election in one constituency had been suspended. Of those eligible, 343 participated in the presidential election.Why Bangladesh needed a new presidentThe election was held after Mohammed Shahabuddin resigned as President on July 24, citing serious health problems.Shahabuddin had been serving as Bangladesh's 22nd President since April 2023, when he was elected unopposed as the nominee of the then-ruling Awami League. His five-year term was originally due to end in April 2028.He submitted his resignation to then-Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed, who assumed the President's constitutional duties under Article 54 until a successor could be elected.Under Bangladesh's Constitution, a new President must be elected by Parliament within 90 days of the office becoming vacant. Thursday's election was therefore held within the required period, ending the temporary arrangement under which the Speaker had been performing the President's duties.From BNP leadership to the presidencyAlamgir's election marks a major change in his political role. He had served as BNP Secretary General before stepping down to contest the presidential election.The result also comes at a significant point in Bangladesh's political transition, with the BNP now holding power after years of opposition politics. Alamgir's move from the party's organisational leadership to the country's highest constitutional office places a senior BNP figure at the head of state.The President's role in Bangladesh is largely constitutional and ceremonial, while executive authority rests with the government headed by the Prime Minister.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
