articles.title: Texas man who made his fortune selling vacuums, bought 5,500 acres in 1969 and spent 40 years restoring its grasslands, water and wildlife
articles.summary: US News: A drive through the Texas Hill Country can make the landscape appear almost timeless. Limestone ridges rise above open grassland, scattered trees brea.
articles.body: A drive through the Texas Hill Country can make the landscape appear almost timeless. Limestone ridges rise above open grassland, scattered trees break up the horizon and streams cut through the valleys. But the appearance can hide a very different history.When J. David Bamberger went looking for ranchland in 1969, he was not interested in buying a beautiful, finished property. He wanted what he called the worst piece of land he could find. As reported by Selah Bamberger Ranch Preserve, he eventually bought 3,000 acres in Blanco County, near Johnson City, with a very specific purpose: to see whether badly overgrazed and neglected land could be brought back to functional health. Over the years, he added adjoining parcels until the property reached 5,500 acres. What followed became one of Texas' largest private habitat restoration projects. The transformation would take decades, requiring patience, careful management and a willingness to let damaged ecosystems gradually recover on their own terms. His remarkable vision proved that even the most degraded landscapes could be revived through determination, demonstrating conservation principles that continue inspiring landowners across Texas today.How Bamberger turned a fortune from business into a decades-long Texas land restoration projectBamberger's path to the Texas Hill Country was unusual. Born in rural Ohio in 1928, he grew up in poverty and developed an early interest in nature and land restoration through his mother, Hester.She gave him Louis Bromfield's Pleasant Valley, a book about restoring a worn-out farm. The story stayed with him. Years later, when Bamberger had built enough financial security to pursue his own ambitions, the idea returned in a very different setting.Reportedly, after moving to Texas with his young family in 1950, Bamberger worked as a vacuum cleaner salesman. He eventually went into business with fellow salesman Bill Church, helping build what became Church's Fried Chicken. When the company went public in 1969, Bamberger became wealthy enough to pursue his long-held ambition of restoring damaged land. Rather than spending his money on a polished ranch, he went looking for land that had already been pushed beyond its productive limits.Turning damaged ranchland into healthy habitatThe property Bamberger found had been heavily affected by years of grazing. Ashe juniper, commonly called cedar locally, had become widespread, while native grasses were scarce. Erosion had damaged the soil, and the ranch had virtually no usable surface water.The land was so dry that Bamberger tried drilling wells. Seven wells, each reaching about 500 feet, failed to produce water. The problem appeared to be much larger than simply finding a new water source. The landscape itself had lost much of its ability to capture and retain rainfall.The restoration team selectively removed Ashe juniper, replanted native grasses and altered the way the land was managed. Terraces and other water-management measures helped slow runoff, giving rainfall more opportunity to soak into the ground.The aim was not to eliminate every tree or turn the ranch into an artificial grassland. It was to create a wider mixture of habitats, including grasslands, oak savannah, riparian areas and remaining cedar thickets. Today, about 15 per cent of the preserve remains cedar thicket.How healthier land brought dormant springs back to lifeOne of the clearest signs that the restoration was working came from underground. As native grasses returned and runoff was reduced, long-dormant springs began flowing again. The preserve now has numerous springs, ponds and other water sources, and Miller Creek originates on the property before flowing toward the Pedernales River and eventually the Colorado River.The main spring produces an average of about three gallons of water per minute, enough to supply the ranch's water needs. Its overflow, together with other springs and seeps, contributes to the headwaters of Miller Creek. That made the project more than a story about restoring a scenic ranch. The preserve's restoration has been recognised by organisations including the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, which awarded Bamberger the Lone Star Land Steward recognition, as well as the Leopold Conservation Award and other conservation organisations.Wildlife returned as the habitat changedThe transformation was also visible in the animals using the property. Early bird surveys in the late 1960s and early 1970s recorded fewer than 50 species. As reported, the preserve's current records list 221 bird species, a dramatic increase that the ranch uses as one measure of improving habitat conditions.The recovery was not limited to birds. White-tailed deer on the original ranch were described as small and unhealthy because the available forage was limited. Bamberger's own account recorded average field-dressed weights of about 55 pounds in the early years. With greater habitat diversity and improved forage, bucks later averaged around 120 pounds, with a 156-pound record reported in 2013.The change reflected something deeper than larger animals. The ranch was producing a broader range of food and shelter, allowing wildlife to use different parts of the landscape throughout the year.How habitat restoration brought endangered species backAs the habitat improved, Bamberger began looking at species that needed more than simply a healthier landscape. The preserve provides habitat for the endangered golden-cheeked warbler and the black-capped vireo. Neither species had been documented on the ranch before restoration began, while nesting pairs of golden-cheeked warblers have since been repeatedly recorded there.The ranch also became involved in the conservation of the scimitar-horned oryx, an antelope that had disappeared from the wild in the Sahara. Bamberger maintained a managed population and worked with zoos, including exchanges of breeding males intended to help maintain genetic diversity. Another unusual project involved bats.The artificial cave that sat empty for yearsIn 1998, Bamberger built a large artificial cave into a hillside for Mexican free-tailed bats. The structure was designed to accommodate as many as a million bats. But construction did not mean the animals would automatically arrive. For years, the cave remained empty. Hundreds of thousands of Mexican free-tailed bats began using the structure during the summer. The cave was named the Chiroptorium, a reference to Chiroptera, the scientific order that contains bats.The project captured the broader philosophy behind the ranch. Bamberger was not simply trying to preserve whatever remained. He was experimenting with ways to create conditions under which wildlife could return and thrive.The ranch became a classroom for other landownersBy the time the transformation was well established, the preserve had become more than a private restoration project. Its mission expanded toward education, research and land stewardship. The preserve now describes itself as a place where landowners can learn conservation-oriented management by seeing the results on the ground. It hosts workshops, educational programmes, research partnerships and tours.His own financial success gave him the ability to take on a 5,500-acre project, but he argued that smaller landowners could apply the same principles. Removing unwanted growth, planting native species, improving water retention and using available equipment could all make a difference. The central idea was patience.What began in 1969 became a conservation legacyIn 2002, Bamberger and his wife, Margaret, established the Bamberger Ranch Preserve as a nonprofit organisation to protect the property from future development and maintain its conservation and educational work. The ranch continues to operate as a research and education resource as well as a restored landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Iran rejects Trump's Hormuz 'total control' claim, says strait will reopen only on Tehran's terms
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran has pushed back against US President Donald Trump’s repeated claims that Washington has “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran in.
articles.body: Iran has pushed back against US President Donald Trump’s repeated claims that Washington has “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran insisting that the strategically vital waterway remains under Iranian control and will not be fully reopened to international shipping unless the US meets its demands.Iranian consul general in Mumbai Saeid Reza Mosayeb Motlagh told ANI on Thursday that Trump’s claim was “false”, rejecting his assertion that the US had destroyed Iran’s naval and missile forces.Motlagh said Tehran was prepared to reopen the strait once Washington fulfilled its commitments and accepted Iran’s conditions under a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).Trump had said on Tuesday that the US had “total control” over the strait through its naval blockade and backed the idea of declaring the strategic waterway US territory.He also claimed the passage remained open and said Iran could still try to disrupt shipping by laying mines. The comments came as Washington continued to use control of the waterway as a major source of pressure on Tehran.Motlagh said any arrangement on Hormuz would have to protect Iran as well as countries along the southern shores of the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. He said Tehran would not accept any agreement that caused damage to Iranian territory.Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has separately said the strait would remain closed to full international shipping until Washington fulfils the commitments outlined in the MoU. These include lifting the US blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending threats and military operations against Iran.Ghalibaf also described Washington's actions as a “breach of covenant” and warned that Iran was prepared to mount a renewed military response if it considered the ceasefire understanding violated.Trump widens pressure campaignThe latest dispute over Hormuz comes as Trump has announced a new economic offensive against Iran, warning that countries providing Tehran with “any type of lifeline” could face “tremendous” economic consequences.Trump said the US was preparing what he described as the “most crushing” economic operation ever imposed on a country, targeting financial and commercial support that could help Iran withstand the pressure. He did not immediately specify which countries or entities would face penalties.The warning raises the prospect of pressure on countries and businesses that continue trading with Iran, as Washington seeks to combine the naval blockade with tighter economic isolation. Iran, meanwhile, has continued to reject US claims over Hormuz and tied any full reopening of the waterway to a broader set of political and economic concessions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Japan installed a 1.1 MW turbine beneath the Naru Strait, using predictable tidal currents to generate clean electricity for the Goto Islands
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru .
articles.body: Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru Strait, a 1.1 MW turbine is drawing energy from water moving with the tides and sending electricity back towards land through a subsea cable. No blades are turning in the sky and no panels spread across the shoreline. The machine works largely out of sight, following currents whose timing can be forecast well in advance. Installed by Proteus Marine Renewables, the AR1100 grew from an earlier 500 kW trial in the same waters. Its deployment has given Japan a megawatt-scale tidal system designed to work with the regular rise and fall of the sea rather than depending on sunshine or changing winds.The project also demonstrates the potential of tidal power in narrow channels, where fast-moving water can provide a concentrated source of renewable energy. By placing the turbine underwater, the system avoids taking up large areas of land while tapping into a resource that follows a predictable natural cycle. Unlike solar and wind power, tidal energy has one major advantage: its timing can be predicted years ahead because tides follow the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun. That predictability could make tidal turbines useful alongside renewable sources whose output changes with weather conditions.How Japan’s 1.1 MW AR1100 tidal turbine generates electricity underwaterThe AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection. According to Proteus Marine Renewables, the turbine was deployed in February 2025, while later company information recorded that it received Japanese certification and began exporting electricity to the grid in June 2025.The arrangement is fairly straightforward in principle, although operating it beneath the sea is not. The rotor extracts energy from moving water, the drivetrain passes that mechanical power to a permanent-magnet generator, and the resulting electricity is carried to an onshore station. A yaw system turns the nacelle as the tidal flow reverses, while independently controlled blades can alter their pitch to regulate how the turbine responds to changing conditions. AR1100 is a horizontal-axis turbine mounted on a gravity-based support structure. The earlier project in the same strait provided the starting point for the larger machine.Japan’s tidal energy project grows from a 500 kW pilot to a 1.1 MW turbineOffshore Energy reported that the earlier 500 kW AR500 pilot operated in the Naru Strait with 97% availability in 2021. That earlier machine had a rated capacity of 500 kW and recorded 97% availability during its operation, according to the material released about the project. The experience allowed engineers to see how the technology behaved in the actual marine environment rather than only in controlled testing.The next version increased the rated capacity to 1.1 MW and introduced changes to the turbine's control systems. An equipment supply and works contract with Kyuden Mirai Energy was signed in November 2022, with the Japanese project subsequently moving towards the upgraded machine. Advanced pitch and yaw systems were incorporated as part of the work. The company says those changes were intended to improve the turbine's performance and efficiency while allowing it to deal more effectively with the changing direction of the tidal flow.Why predictable tidal energy could complement solar and wind in JapanThe most distinctive feature of tidal power is not simply that the turbines sit underwater. It is the predictability of the resource. Solar output changes with daylight and weather conditions. Wind can strengthen, weaken or stop altogether. ClickPetroleogas noted that tidal production can be estimated in advance because the cycles follow predictable natural patterns, unlike renewable generation that is more affected by weather conditions. The electricity produced at any particular moment still depends on the conditions at the site and the performance of the equipment; the underlying movement of the water is far less of a surprise.That distinction matters when renewable sources are being combined. A grid operator cannot make the sun shine or order the wind to blow, whereas the timing of tidal cycles can be incorporated into generation planning. It does not make tidal energy constant; the flow rises and falls as the tide changes, but it makes the pattern easier to anticipate. For islands such as those around the Goto group, where space and fuel logistics can present particular constraints, a submerged source can sit alongside solar, wind and other forms of generation. The Naru Strait project is intended to contribute to reducing emissions from the islands' electricity supply.The engineering challenges of operating a tidal turbine underwaterUnderwater generation creates its own engineering problems. Components have to survive saltwater, strong currents and long periods of exposure while remaining accessible enough for inspection and maintenance. Getting people and equipment to a submerged turbine can also require vessels, specialist crews and careful planning. The location itself has to provide sufficient water movement, suitable depth and a practical route for sending the electricity into the grid.The Naru Strait project therefore depends on more than the turbine turning. Its subsea cable links the machine to an onshore electrical station, where the generated power can be processed for distribution. Local vessels and resources were used during deployment, with Proteus' offshore team overseeing the work, while Kyuden Mirai Energy and Japan's Ministry of Environment have been involved in advancing the project.There is also a useful way to think about the long-term promise of the machine, without treating its output as something that can be guaranteed hour by hour. The tidal timetable itself is highly predictable. Engineers can calculate when stronger and weaker currents are expected well into the future, creating a generation pattern that can be plotted ahead of time. What cannot simply be printed on that chart is the turbine's actual electricity production for every future hour: maintenance, operating conditions and other technical factors still matter.That distinction is important. The Naru Strait turbine is not a giant power station, nor does the available source material establish that it will produce a fixed amount of electricity every hour for a decade. What the project demonstrates is something more specific: a megawatt-scale machine can be installed beneath a Japanese strait, connected to shore and operated using an energy source whose basic timing is known far in advance. The water will keep changing direction. The turbine is built to follow it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1968, one man left modern life behind, built a remote Alaska cabin himself and spent nearly 30 years living in the wilderness
articles.summary: US News: Most people notice how much they rely on modern life only when something stops working. A broken heater, an empty fridge or a lost internet connection.
articles.body: Most people notice how much they rely on modern life only when something stops working. A broken heater, an empty fridge or a lost internet connection can quickly turn an ordinary day into an inconvenience. Richard Proenneke chose to live with far fewer conveniences, and he built the place that would become his home accordingly.In the remote Alaskan wilderness, there was no hardware store around the corner when a tool failed or a building needed repair. Proenneke worked with hand tools, local wood and whatever materials he could make useful. His cabin at Upper Twin Lake was small, but almost every part of it reflected careful thought about living alone in a demanding landscape.The story of the cabin is therefore about more than logs and a roof. It is about patience, resourcefulness and the quiet determination to make everyday life work with what is already at hand, there. Every cut, joint and improvised solution carried the practical lessons of someone learning to depend less on convenience and more on his surroundings. Even simple tasks demanded planning, steady effort and an understanding of the changing weather, making the cabin as much a survival system as a home.Richard Proenneke built his Alaska cabin with hand tools and local woodProenneke did not arrive at Twin Lakes with a complete collection of modern equipment. He brought certain steel components for his tools and fashioned wooden handles from material available around him. Much of the work was then done with those basic implements.That approach extended beyond the building itself. When a tool broke, replacing it was not the automatic answer. He repaired it and continued using it. The cabin therefore reflects not just the materials available in the Alaskan bush, but a way of working in which useful objects were kept going for as long as possible.As reported by the National Park Service (NPS), the building is about 12 feet wide and 16 feet long. Its walls are made from peeled spruce logs, with the corners joined through carefully cut saddle notches. It has three windows, each made with thin plastic rather than conventional glass, and a small fireplace constructed from stones gathered locally.The entrance is a handmade Dutch door. Its wooden hinges and lock are among the smaller features that reveal how much attention went into ordinary parts of the structure.Moss, soil and grass gradually transformed the cabin’s roofThe original roof was covered with moss collected from within a short distance of the cabin. It seemed an appropriate material for a home surrounded by forest, but the conditions at Twin Lakes presented a problem.Moss needs considerable moisture to remain healthy. The relatively dry environment meant that it did not thrive as a roof covering in the way Proenneke had hoped. Over the years he kept adding material, eventually producing a thin layer made up of moss, earth and grass.It was not a single finished job so much as something that developed with the cabin. More than 30 years of additions left the roof with a natural-looking covering that became part of the building's character.Why Proenneke built his storage cache nine feet above the groundThe cabin was only one part of the small settlement Proenneke created for himself. Eleven feet away stood a raised cache for storing supplies.The structure measured roughly 6 by 4 feet and was made from peeled spruce logs. It rested on poles about nine feet high, considerably taller than the traditional caches commonly found in nearby Athabascan communities. There was a practical reason for the difference. Traditional caches were often situated in populated places, where people and dogs provided some deterrence against wildlife. Proenneke expected to be living alone. Raising the storage structure higher reduced the chances of a bear reaching what was kept inside.A ladder made from local materials provided access. Tin wrapped around the supporting poles served another purpose, making it difficult for smaller animals to climb up. The design was simple, but it showed that the buildings were being shaped around the realities of the landscape rather than simply copied from elsewhere.The overlooked building near the cabinAbout 45 feet east of the cabin was a second structure combining a woodshed and an outhouse. Its main section was used for storing tools and keeping a supply of firewood close at hand. Proenneke was careful not to allow his woodpile to run too low, an understandable precaution in a place where heating and cooking depended on what could be gathered and stored.The building followed the basic form of an Adirondack shelter, with a sloping roof. At one end was an outhouse, about 33 inches wide, with a half-moon opening carved into its door. There was a small practical compromise behind its use. Proenneke kept the facility available for visitors rather than having to rebuild or relocate an outhouse repeatedly for their sake. When alone, he generally went into the surrounding woods instead.A home built around self-relianceProenneke's life at the lake was not supported by electricity, running water or a telephone. For roughly 30 years, the cabin remained a place where everyday needs had to be handled without the infrastructure found in ordinary homes.That makes the construction itself more revealing. The cabin was not simply a shelter erected and then left behind. Its maintenance, heating, storage and gradual repairs were all tied to the same self-reliant system.The surrounding site also had paths leading towards the lake, connecting the buildings with the shoreline. From above, the arrangement looks small: a cabin, raised cache and woodshed among the trees. On the ground, each part had a defined purpose.The cabin and the man behind itThere is another reason Proenneke's cabin remains distinctive. He documented its construction on film. The record provides an unusually direct view of how the building took shape and of the techniques he used. Rather than leaving behind only a finished cabin, Proenneke preserved evidence of the work involved in making it.That documentation also helped give the site a place in the wider story of wilderness life in Alaska. The cabin itself was not the largest or earliest bush cabin in the state. Its significance came from the combination of craftsmanship, self-sufficiency and the record Proenneke left behind.A photograph taken in 1985 shows him sitting in the doorway, dressed in a blue flannel shirt and brown trousers. By then the cabin had already been standing for many years, but it still looked closely connected to the surroundings that had shaped its construction.A small site with a larger historical recordThe cabin and its associated buildings were added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2007. The recognition reflects the site's importance as an example of an Alaskan bush log cabin, as well as Proenneke's role in documenting and communicating ideas about wilderness preservation.The setting matters as much as the buildings. The cabin was made from spruce taken from the area, its storage arrangements were adapted to local wildlife, and its roof changed in response to the climate. Even small decisions were influenced by the conditions around Upper Twin Lake.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: A fresh social media post has reignited the dispute between Candace Owens, Erika Kirk and Turning Point USA over the public narrative surrounding Tyler Robinson’s case. Grace Ashford shared a screenshot accusing Erika Kirk and TPUSA of attacking critics who question inconsistencies in the case. The post also points to Owens’ latest comments, placing her at the center of another heated debate over the 22-year-old defendant.Candace Owens faces fresh scrutiny over Erika Kirk and TPUSA claimsThe controversy began with a post from Grace Ashford, who claimed that Erika Kirk and TPUSA had accused critics of being evil for raising questions about the case. Ashford’s post argues that the public deserves answers when statements made by prominent figures later appear inconsistent with information that emerges.The screenshot features a video of Candace Owens discussing the issue. Owens focuses on a previous statement attributed to Erika Kirk concerning whether Charlie Kirk had been sending text messages shortly before his death.Owens argues that a public correction should follow if new information contradicts an earlier claim. She frames accountability as essential to maintaining public trust, particularly when a case has attracted intense attention online.Owens said:“When Erika publicly stated with confidence on Glenn Beck's show that Charlie was not sending text messages the night before signaling that he was worried. He was going to be killed It then becomes incumbent upon Erika herself to correct the record publicly When we learn that that isn't true. That's how you build goodwill with the public take accountability when it comes to Turning Point USA It's just amazing. It's it feels like we're just being perpetually gaslit by them We're offered a biblical proverb like how dare you even ask us to explain why what we told you before is completely inconsistent With what we're saying now, they're just suggesting that we're evil for noticing these various inconsistencies and illogical points That are being presented by them.”Her comments have become part of a wider argument over how much information should be accepted at face value while the legal process is still unfolding.Tyler Robinson case remains at center of public disputeOwens then shifted her focus to Robinson’s legal position and the intense public reaction surrounding his case. She questioned why people connected to TPUSA appeared so determined, in her view, to portray Robinson as guilty before a trial has established that conclusion.She also criticized the use of influencers and commentators to discuss courtroom proceedings, arguing that legal filings should be represented accurately rather than selectively.Owens continued:“Why I don't know if it needs reminding but in this country it is innocent until proven guilty So Why does it seem that Turning Point USA and the representatives and their affiliates are so hell-bent on sending a 22 year old young Man to his death. He's up for the death sentence Why are they bringing influencers into the courtroom? Why are they as Blake Neff has done repeatedly completely Misrepresenting court filings to the public in order to do just that To assert that Tyler Robinson is guilty.""This is a tweet by the way from just this morning from Blakey just Lies and misrepresents and we're the bad guys for noticing that he's doing it. This is what the tweet read. He wrote Utah prosecutors have responded to Tyler Robinson's defense filing ahead of the final preliminary hearing and Confirms what observers pointed out about that filing the defense is very conspicuously not contesting any of the core evidence showing Tyler Robinson committed the murder.""They don't contest the camera footage the DNA the rifle the cause of death or Tyler's phone data All they have is a complaint about reliable hearsay Which won't apply at the full trial anyway, and then attacks on the aggravating factors If there was any merit at all to any of the theories that Candace and them have pushed the last 11 months Why didn't the defense bring them up? It's stunning to me that he thinks he can get away with this it says Preliminary hearings decide only probable cause under the Utah 1102 standard reliable hearsay is allowed defense counsel often skip alternative theories To avoid previewing their strategy before the trial silence does not prove that those theories lack merit”The remarks highlight the sharp divide surrounding the case. Owens is questioning how Robinson’s defense strategy and court filings are being interpreted publicly, while critics argue that the available evidence should be taken seriously.A key distinction remains important: allegations and arguments made by commentators are not the same as findings by a court. Robinson’s guilt must ultimately be determined through the legal process, and public commentary cannot replace that process.The viral screenshot has therefore become another flashpoint in an already intense dispute. It does not resolve the competing claims, but it shows how deeply divided the public conversation has become around Erika Kirk, TPUSA, Candace Owens and the Tyler Robinson case.As proceedings continue, the evidence presented in court will carry far greater weight than competing narratives on social media. For now, the online battle over what happened, what was said and what the public should believe shows no sign of slowing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 55,000 years ago, Neanderthals may have trekked deep into Saudi Arabia when Nefud Desert was covered by lakes and grasslands
articles.summary: Middle East News: A new study suggests Neanderthals may have trekked far deeper into the Arabian Peninsula than scientists previously thought possible, reaching a lakes.
articles.body: A new study suggests Neanderthals may have trekked far deeper into the Arabian Peninsula than scientists previously thought possible, reaching a lakeside site in what is now Saudi Arabia around 55,000 years ago. Researchers examined stone tools from Jebel Katefeh 1, a site beside an ancient lake near the city of Jubbah in the Nefud Desert. No Neanderthal bones or DNA have ever been found in Arabia, so the team relied on the shape of stone flakes to identify who made them. Using a statistical model built from sites with well-established toolmakers, researchers found the tools far more closely resembled those made by Neanderthals than by early Homo sapiens toolmakers nearby. New dating work narrowed the age of the site to about 55,000 years, a period when the desert was becoming wetter and greener, and Neanderthals were the only hominin group known to inhabit southwest Asia at that time. This groundbreaking research fundamentally challenges long-held assumptions about Neanderthal capabilities and mobility, suggesting our ancient relatives were far more adaptable and widely dispersed than previously imagined.How researchers identified Neanderthal stone tools in the Nefud DesertLacking bones or ancient DNA, the research team turned to the physical shape of stone flakes struck from carefully prepared cores, a technique that can preserve distinctive differences between toolmaking groups. The findings, published in the study Neanderthals in the desert? Population history best explains Middle Palaeolithic technological heterogeneity in Arabia, describe how the team measured hundreds of flakes from Jebel Katefeh 1 and a smaller nearby site called ALM 3. Researchers then compared them statistically against tools from other locations across Arabia, the Levant and northeast Africa where the identity of the toolmakers was already established. This comparison allowed the researchers to build a model capable of distinguishing patterns associated with Neanderthal toolmaking from those associated with early Homo sapiens. Because no human remains were recovered from Jebel Katefeh 1, the statistical analysis is central to the study's argument that Neanderthals, rather than another hominin population, were responsible for producing the tools.Why the discovery pushes the Neanderthal range farther south than expectedNeanderthals have traditionally been associated with Europe and other relatively cool environments, but archaeological discoveries over the past two decades have substantially expanded their known geographical range. Evidence has placed Neanderthals thousands of miles eastward into Siberia and across parts of the Middle East, while the new study suggests they may also have ventured deep into the Arabian interior. Establishing when people occupied Jebel Katefeh 1 was therefore crucial. Researchers excavated a new trench and used optically stimulated luminescence, a dating technique that measures when mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight, to establish the age of the sediment. The tools were recovered from a layer marking a transition between older desert sand and younger lake sediment, placing the occupation at a time when environmental conditions were changing. Around 55,000 years ago, parts of Arabia periodically became substantially wetter than they are today, creating lakes, grasslands and other habitats capable of supporting large populations of grazing animals. Those temporary green conditions may have opened routes through landscapes that are now among the driest places on Earth.What outside experts think about the evidence for Neanderthals in ArabiaIndependent archaeologists have described the evidence as compelling, while emphasising that the identification remains based on indirect archaeological evidence rather than human remains. Knut Bretzke, an archaeologist at the University of Tübingen who was not involved in the research, said the case for a Neanderthal presence in northern Arabia was strong and suggested that wetter conditions could have attracted grazing animals into the desert interior, potentially providing a reason for Neanderthals to follow them. He also noted that several sites used in the statistical comparison were surface sites, meaning their stone tools could have accumulated over extended periods rather than representing a single occupation. That limitation makes the precise interpretation of technological differences important. Study co-lead author Huw Groucutt, an archaeologist at the University of Malta, has likewise acknowledged that a Neanderthal fossil would provide much stronger confirmation. However, bones and ancient DNA are particularly difficult to preserve in Arabia's harsh environment, leaving stone tools as one of the few surviving traces of human activity. If the interpretation is correct, the Jebel Katefeh evidence suggests Neanderthals were capable of travelling much farther into Arabia's changing landscapes than previously documented, following temporary lakes and wildlife across an environment that today appears almost completely inhospitable to human settlement.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Four workers carrying out weed-control work on a railway track in Japan were killed after they were struck by an express train as it entered Shin-Kanuma Station, north of Tokyo.The collision occurred around 10.46 am (local time) on Thursday while the workers were spraying herbicide on the railway track, according to Tobu Railway, which operates the line.Police are investigating whether proper safety procedures were followed at the time of the accident, railway officials said at a press conference.Train services on the Tobu Nikko Line were suspended following the incident.The four men, three workers and a supervisor, were taken to hospital after the collision but were later pronounced dead, police and train operator Tobu Railway Co. said.Six others at the site, including two workers, three people assigned to lookout duty and another supervisor, were unharmed, according to Tobu Railway.The four workers, who were in their 50s and 60s, were part of a 10-member team carrying out work at the site, railway officials said. The team included a supervisor and three lookouts responsible for warning workers of approaching trains.The lookouts typically use whistles and microphones to alert workers, while also waving a yellow flag to signal the train driver.However, when repeatedly asked whether anyone had been keeping watch for approaching trains before the collision, railway officials did not provide a clear answer.A Tobu Railway representative had earlier told the BBC that the "usual lookout system was operating as normal". "When a train approaches, a lookout waves a flag and, once the driver acknowledges it, sounds the horn," he said."We are currently investigating why the accident occurred despite this."Train services on the Tobu Nikko Line were suspended following the accident, according to Tobu Railway.A passenger aboard the train told Japanese public broadcaster NHK that they heard a "strange noise" before the train made an emergency stop. The passenger said those on board remained on the train for some time as staff announced that they were investigating the source of the noise, as cited by the BBC.Fatal train accidents are relatively rare in Japan, despite the country’s extensive railway network. articles.title: In 2019, Bahrain sank a 70-metre Boeing 747 in 20–22 metres of water; the jumbo jet became the centrepiece of a 100,000-square-metre underwater park
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In an innovative approach to marine tourism, Bahrain has transformed a retired Boeing 747 into the centerpiece of Dive Bahrain, a 100,000-square-meter underwater park aimed at promoting diving, marine research, and conservation efforts.
articles.body: In June 2019, a Boeing 747 made an unusual final journey in Bahrain. Instead of heading to an aircraft graveyard, the 70-metre-long jumbo jet was towed out to sea and lowered onto the seabed to become the centrepiece of Dive Bahrain, a 100,000-square-metre underwater park. Bahrain turned a retired passenger aircraft into both a tourist attraction and an artificial marine structure.According to the Bahrain Ministry of Industry and Commerce, the underwater park was developed not only as a diving attraction but also as a site for marine research and environmental education. The Boeing 747 formed the centrepiece of the initial 100,000-square-metre park, while later phases were planned to add artificial reefs, sculptures and a replica of a traditional Bahraini pearl merchant's house. These planned additions were intended to expand the site's marine habitat while also connecting the attraction with Bahrain's maritime heritage.From airport aircraft to artificial reefGetting a jumbo jet underwater was itself a considerable engineering exercise. The retired aircraft was prepared for submersion, transported to the purpose-built dive site and carefully lowered into the sea. Bahrain’s Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Tourism states that the Boeing 747, measuring 70 metres in length, was placed 20 to 22 metres below the surface north of Bahrain, becoming the first attraction in the 100,000-square-metre Dive Bahrain park. The aircraft was not simply placed on the seabed as a spectacle. Its large surfaces, openings and sheltered spaces also created hard surfaces that marine organisms could colonise, while fish and other species could use the structure for shelter.According to Frontiers in Marine Science, a global meta-analysis of 39 studies found that artificial reefs can support fish communities with levels of density, biomass, species richness and diversity comparable to those found on natural reefs. The researchers also stressed that their effectiveness depends on factors such as location and construction material. In Bahrain, this provides a useful context for the decision to combine the aircraft with other artificial structures across the dive park. Together, these features give the site a broader ecological role.A park built around more than a planeOn 8 September 2019, Dive Bahrain officially opened its 100,000-square-metre underwater site, with the submerged Boeing 747 serving as its first major attraction. The government said later phases would add a replica of a traditional Bahraini pearl merchant's house, artificial coral reefs and other sculptures. These structures were intended to create new surfaces for marine organisms to colonise while giving divers more features to explore. The inclusion of the pearl merchant's house was particularly fitting for Bahrain, whose maritime history is closely tied to pearl diving. The underwater park therefore combined an important part of the country's heritage with a modern marine tourism attraction.The presence of artificial structures, however, does not by itself guarantee the development of a healthy coral ecosystem. Their location, materials, design and surrounding environmental conditions can all influence which organisms settle on them and how those communities develop. A review published in PLOS One found that artificial reefs can provide surfaces for coral recruitment and habitat for marine organisms, but their ecological outcomes vary considerably. The researchers also noted that many projects are either too small or monitored for too short a period to establish whether they deliver broader conservation benefits. For Dive Bahrain, this means the value of the park will depend not simply on what was placed on the seabed, but on how these structures function as habitat over time.From spectacle to long-term experimentBahrain’s environmental authorities said Dive Bahrain could support marine ecology and biology research while raising public awareness about conservation. By allowing divers to see how marine organisms colonised submerged structures, the site was also intended to provide an accessible way to engage visitors with marine ecosystems. At the same time, the government viewed the project as a means of expanding diving tourism in Bahrain.The 747 therefore became more than a sunken aircraft. It formed the first part of a wider project intended to bring together tourism, environmental education and the development of artificial marine habitat. After spending its working life carrying passengers around the world, the aircraft was given a second purpose beneath the sea. It became the centrepiece of an underwater attraction where recreation and marine-focused development were brought together.The park also provided an unusual setting for observing how artificial structures changed after being placed underwater. As algae, corals, sponges and other organisms settled on exposed surfaces, the appearance of the aircraft and surrounding installations could change over time. This gradual transformation made the site different from a conventional diving attraction, because the underwater landscape was expected to develop as marine life interacted with the structures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Apollo 11 set up the Moon's first seismometer in 1969; its recorded moonquakes gave scientists the first detailed map of the lunar interior
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Apollo 11's groundbreaking seismometer laid the foundation for lunar seismology, revealing the Moon's internal structure and enabling future explorations.
articles.body: When Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Sea of Tranquility in July 1969, they deployed several scientific instruments during their moonwalk, including one designed not to study rocks or footprints but to detect seismic activity on the Moon. It was a seismometer, the first instrument placed on another world to detect the equivalent of earthquakes. That single, short-lived experiment marked the beginning of lunar seismology, a field that eventually let scientists build a detailed picture of what lies beneath the Moon's surface, though it took data from several later missions, not Apollo 11 alone, to complete that picture.The instrument Armstrong and Aldrin deployed was called the Passive Seismic Experiment. As described on NASA's official science page for the device, it packed four separate seismometers, three long-period sensors and one short-period vertical sensor, into a single unit powered by two solar panels. The device was also sensitive enough to measure the vibrations produced by the movement of the astronauts as well as the activities of people around the lander. When activated, it sent seismic measurements back to receiving stations on Earth, enabling researchers to examine the magnitude, duration, and origin of the events.Because it was powered by sunlight and lacked thermal control, it could operate only during lunar daytime. This, along with the intense lunar noon heat, ended the experiment. NASA's report states that the instrument package ceased responding to commands at 0400 UT on 25 August 1969, probably due to overheating.Short but memorable periodTwenty days might seem insignificant, but that period was enough to show that seismology could be applied to other celestial bodies. In its description of the scientific findings from the Apollo program, NASA mentions that the Passive Seismic Experiment discovered moonquakes and provided scientists with information about the internal structure of the Moon, as summarized on NASA's astrobiology mission page. During its short operational life, the same instrument detected an estimated 100 to 200 meteorite impacts, while the later Apollo network detected 1,700 meteoroid impacts over a longer service period.Recognizing the value of the short dataset, NASA developed improved designs for the instrument. The later seismometers were powered by radioisotope thermoelectric generators, fitted with improved thermal regulation, and installed at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, and 16 landing sites. In contrast to the Apollo 11 instrument, the more advanced seismometers deployed at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, and 16 landing sites operated as a long-duration network and transmitted data to Earth until September 1977, according to the NASA Astrobiology mission page for Apollo 11.Constructing the detailed mapThe map we have today of the Moon’s interior was built from this joint effort, which began with Apollo 11. NASA technical report from the mission's science teams, Results From the Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment, available through the NASA Technical Reports Server, documents how researchers used the accumulated seismic data to trace how energy from moonquakes and impacts traveled through the Moon's crust, mantle, and core, revealing a layered interior with a crust, mantle, and core, while also showing that the Moon is smaller, less seismically active, and thermally more evolved than Earth.Over almost eight years, this network recorded many thousands of seismic events, including deep and shallow moonquakes, artificial impulses, and more than a thousand meteoroid impacts. The most common type of moonquake was the deep kind, which occurred hundreds of kilometers below the surface and repeated at specific phases of the Moon’s tidal cycle. Another, rarer type of moonquake was the shallow kind, which occurred closer to the surface and may have been caused by tectonic activity within the lunar crust. Analysis of wave propagation and attenuation helped scientists understand the thickness of the lunar crust, distinguish it from the mantle below, and detect the presence of a tiny core inside the Moon, information that could not have been discovered by Apollo 11 alone in just 20 days.A timeless basis for continued discoveriesMore than fifty years later, the information gained from Apollo 11’s initial measurements and the subsequent missions remains a source of discovery. Modern researchers re-evaluate the old records using up-to-date methods of computation, finding signals that were not analyzed properly before. While Armstrong and Aldrin’s passive seismology experiment during their first spacewalk on the Moon was small-scale and short-lived, it helped launch an entire field of study.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, students helped raise money to protect a Canadian island from development; Chip Wilson’s family foundation later donated C$4 million to protect three islands
articles.summary: In a remarkable story of community activism and philanthropy, a British Columbia charity, backed by students and billionaire Chip Wilson, successfully raised C$4 million to protect three endangered islands from development. Discover how grassroots efforts and private donations led to one of the largest conservation gifts in Canadian history.
articles.body: In 2020, a small British Columbia charity gave itself an almost impossible deadline: it had to raise enough money to buy a private island before its owner sold it to developers. What began as a modest local campaign, boosted in part by a group of high school students, eventually led to a major conservation gift after Lululemon founder Chip Wilson agreed to match every dollar raised.A race against the clockThe area in question was West Ballenas Island, an estimated 100‑acre stretch of rocky, forested terrain in the Strait of Georgia, 15 kilometres north of Nanaimo. The BC Parks Foundation, established in 2017, is an independent charitable partner of BC Parks that works to protect valuable places across British Columbia. The foundation had only days left to raise the C$1.7 million needed to acquire the island, as reported in a BC Govt News release on the province’s parks protection and nature conservation efforts.The man behind the matchFor several months, the donor remained anonymous. The matching funds later turned out to have come from the Wilson 5 Foundation, the family charitable trust of Chip Wilson and his wife, Shannon. In 2021, the foundation donated C$4 million toward protecting 365 acres of threatened Coastal Douglas-fir habitat on Lasqueti Island, Saturna Island, and West Ballenas Island.Wilson's interest in conservation traced back to a visit to Vancouver's Stanley Park, where he said he was impressed by the vision of whoever had set aside the land many years earlier. He said he wanted to be able to do something similar for his family in the future. All three properties lie in the Salish Sea and contain rare Coastal Douglas-fir ecosystems, including old-growth forest and Garry oak meadows.Why these islands matterThe Coastal Douglas-fir ecosystem preserved by these islands is among the most threatened ecosystems in British Columbia. The BC Parks Foundation described the C$4 million contribution as the largest contribution it had ever received. As per CBC News Canada, this milestone would later be surpassed by contributions from the Wilsons themselves. In 2022, the Wilson 5 Foundation donated C$100 million to the BC Parks Foundation to support the launch of its 25x25 campaign, a multi‑year initiative to protect 25% of British Columbia’s land and waters by 2025.Model for conservation fundraisingWhat makes the West Ballenas story remarkable is not just the amount raised, but the process that got it there. Individual students raising almost C$3,000 through a school fundraising campaign could not have stopped the development of an island on their own. By adding to other donations, they helped build the groundswell of support that made a private matching gift possible. Wilson’s foundation helped leverage a campaign started by residents, including teenagers trying to save part of the coastline near their school. The West Ballenas campaign demonstrated how crowdfunding and matching funds could bring together local supporters and major private donors to help protect privately owned conservation lands.Another instance where a shifting strategy has been employed to secure lands for conservation in Canada is the West Ballenas Island campaign. In the case where BC Parks Foundation needed to act fast and there was a $1.7 million shortfall to buy the island, a crowdfunding effort by the community, spearheaded by local students, showed their dedication. This led to the foundation getting a massive donation match from the Wilson 5 Foundation and other private donors, which saw the purchase of the island as well as other islands being protected.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1920s, America turned to Japanese oysters as its native industry declined; their descendants now support a Pacific Northwest shellfish industry worth over $270 million
articles.summary: US News: Discover how the introduction of Japanese Pacific oysters transformed the collapsing oyster industry in America’s Pacific Northwest, contributing over $270 million to the economy.
articles.body: In the late 1910s and 1920s, oyster growers on the US Pacific coast turned to Japan for an unlikely solution to a worsening crisis. The region’s native Olympia oyster industry had declined dramatically after decades of overharvesting, pollution and deteriorating habitat. Growers began importing the Pacific oyster (Crassostrea gigas) from Japan, hoping that a larger, faster-growing oyster species could keep the declining industry alive. Initiated by accidental early shipments, the intentional scaled cultivation of these imports expanded rapidly throughout the 1920s, serving as the foundation of modern West Coast oyster farming. According to NOAA Fisheries, Pacific oysters, or Japanese oysters, were introduced to the United States from Japan in the 1920s and now support a Northwest shellfish industry contributing an estimated $270 million annually to the regional economy.When the native oyster industry began collapsingThe story began with the rapid decline of the Olympia oyster, the only oyster species native to Washington waters. Indigenous populations had harvested these oysters for thousands of years, although the commercial production expanded during the 19th century. The Pacific Shellfish Institute noted that the Olympia oyster industry reached its peak in the 1890s before declining sharply because of overharvesting and deteriorating water quality. By 1915, the native oyster harvests in Puget Sound were almost nonexistent.Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife records show that this ongoing commercial transition became irreversible when sulfite waste from a pulp mill, which opened at Shelton in 1927, severely affected the few remainingnative oyster populations in southern Puget Sound. It is worth noting that over the following decades, ongoing pollution continuously suppressed the reproduction, recruitment, abundance, and growth of native Olympia oysters. This environmental barrier solidified the industry's shift toward the hardier Japanese replacement, thus ensuring the transition became permanent.Notably, growers had already experimented with other species, as reported by several federal archives. Records of West Coast oyster cultivation show that American oysters from the Atlantic coast were introduced into Washington, but survival was poor. Meanwhile, Pacific oysters from Japan offered a more promising alternative because they were better adapted to the region’s conditions and grew rapidly.Japanese oysters arrived in the Pacific Northwest after several failed experiments Historical records reviewed by NOAA show that growers shipped adult oysters from Japan in the early 1900s, while a 1919 shipment of 400 cases from Japan’s Miyagi Prefecture unintentionally carried millions of viable juvenile oyster "spat"- young oysters that had settled and permanently attached themselves to the adult shells. Those surviving seed oystershelped establish Pacific oyster cultivation in Washington’s Samish Bay.However, by the 1920s, importing Pacific oyster seed had become a deliberate strategy for rebuilding commercial oyster production. The imported species proved hardy and became a dominant oyster cultivated on the West Coast. The shift was dramatic: Pacific oysters are substantially larger than the native Olympia oysters and reach market size much faster. NOAA reported that as the species thrives under diverse environmental conditions, it has become a leading aquaculture species on the West Coast. Unlike crops that require feed, farmed oysters obtain their food by directly filtering naturally occurring phytoplankton from seawater, thus making shellfish farming fundamentally different from many forms of livestock or finfish aquaculture.The imported species gradually became naturalised in parts of Washington, with Pacific oysters now established in areas including Puget Sound. They are co-managed as a wild resource by Washington state and Native American tribes. However, while these wild populations maintain self-sustaining numbers for public and tribal harvesting, their spawning cycles fluctuate dramatically based on annual water temperatures. To insulate the commercial economy from this seasonal volatility, modern commercial growers rely heavily on advanced hatcheries to secure a predictable, year-round supply of specialized seed. Today, the legacy of those imported oysters underpins a major coastal economy, as NOAA estimates that the resulting Pacific Northwest shellfish industry contributes $270 million per year to the regional economy and supports more than 3,200 jobs, especially in coastal communities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2021, a flood-prone French town planned a 1.3-megawatt solar roof over its cemetery; the canopy would protect graves, collect water and supply residents
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how the commune of Saint-Joachim in western France is turning its cemetery into a solar energy powerhouse, addressing flooding issues, collecting rainwater, and providing clean electricity to local residents.
articles.body: In the marshland of western France, the commune of Saint-Joachim has been transforming an unlikely site, its municipal cemetery, into an unusual clean-energy project. Located in the Brière marsh near the Loire estuary, the commune began developing the plan in 2021: a photovoltaic canopy intended to generate approximately 1.3 megawatts while reducing flooding and supplying locally shared electricity to the town’s roughly 4,000 residents, according to Fondation de France and pv magazine International. Saint-Joachim, a commune of roughly 4,000 residents in Loire-Atlantique’s Brière marsh, developed a plan for a photovoltaic canopy over its municipal cemetery. As per the Fondation de France, the installation was intended to prevent flooding, collect rainwater for the nearby sports complex, and generate solar electricity for local households, businesses, and an EHPAD through collective self-consumption. It was a direct response to a problem the town had lived with for decades, namely a cemetery that regularly floods.But why a cemetery?In 1970, after the original cemetery near the church became too small, Saint-Joachim built the cemetery that remains in use today. Unlike the previous cemetery, which was six meters above sea level, the new cemetery was located very close to sea level and straight into the middle of the Brière marsh, a giant peat bog. Winter rains regularly submerged the pathways and shallow graves, as detailed in PV Magazine International, and residents struggled to accept the flooding.The wetland could not be permanently drained because the town was built on reclaimed marshland. That led Saint-Joachim’s mayor to propose covering the cemetery and diverting the rainwater. Once the idea of covering the cemetery emerged, solar panels became a natural fit, as the town had already done in 2012, according to the report.The nonprofit Fondation de France, which has followed the project's community-organising model, describes the plan as pursuing three goals at once: preventing flooding, capturing rainwater for irrigation, and producing solar power for the town's roughly 4,000 residents.How it works and how it has evolvedEarly project descriptions placed the installation at roughly 5,000-5,300 panels covering approximately 8,000-8,600 square metres, with a projected capacity of about 1.3 MW. Other reports described the revised design as comprising approximately 5,900 panels, while France Télévisions reported approximately 9,000 square metres of panels and a capacity of about 1.2 MW. The exact final panel count and covered proportion of the cemetery should therefore be treated as provisional unless confirmed by Brièr’Énergie or the municipality. These numbers describe a more advanced stage of the engineering process than a fundamental shift in the concept of the project itself. The town's official municipal bulletin, published by the Mairie de Saint-Joachim, confirmed in its January 2025 edition that the first sections of the canopy had been installed as a test phase over the cemetery.The canopy is designed to perform two functions. First, it is designed to reduce flooding by catching rainwater before it reaches the graves and directing it to an adjacent sports facility for irrigation, as PV Magazine International reported. Second, it is meant to generate energy. The electricity will feed into the public grid through a collective self-consumption model that distributes power among participants. As Fondation de France notes, the coordinating body created an allocation formula to prevent the biggest users from taking too much of the electricity.Two citizen associations, registered with the town and formally listed in France's national business registry, Brier Energie and RECIT, developed the project alongside the municipality. One of the most vocal promoters of the project has been Éric Broquaire, President of Brier'Energie. In an interview with Euronews Green, he said the project appealed because it was based on shared ownership, not just financial returns.Community approval and fundingDue to the cemetery being an important site in an emotional sense, the community approval was seen as an absolute necessity and not just an obligatory step. Letters were sent to all residents requesting approval before construction began, and Euronews Green reported that approval reached 97 percent, though that figure could not be independently confirmed. Fondation de France notes that the electricity was meant to be provided to the citizens for free, as the town itself would cover the installation expenses instead of the citizens.Other reports describe a cheaper way to join the association, but those membership details and panel prices could not be independently confirmed. The municipality planned to finance the €3.35 million installation with additional revenue generated by a 7 percent increase in the property tax, adjusted for inflation, rather than through a separate levy created solely to fund the canopy. pv magazine International makes this distinction clear.Significance of the projectSaint-Joachim’s decision to place solar panels on existing land reflects a broader French trend toward installing them on rooftops, car parks and other already-used sites, including cemeteries. France has also enacted legislation requiring solar canopies in large car parks, making the Saint-Joachim project part of the same national trend.The original target of summer 2025 was later pushed back to 2026. The Mairie de Saint-Joachim’s registration system still asks residents, renters, property owners, and businesses to complete registration so they can receive the electricity. The project turns a persistent local flooding problem at a cemetery into infrastructure that also provides public benefits.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In the Early 1900s, a Maryland landowner released just five or six Japanese sika deer, and their descendants spread across four counties and Assateague Island
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating journey of Japanese sika deer in Maryland, from just five individuals to a thriving population across multiple counties and Assateague Island. Learn about their habitat, impact on local wildlife, and the challenges of managing this non-native species.
articles.body: In 1916, five or six Japanese sika deer were released on James Island in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay. That small introduction became the foundation of a population that would eventually spread across much of the lower Eastern Shore. Sika deer are native to southern Japan, but Maryland's population began with the animals brought to James Island. Maryland's wildlife agency now records sika deer in Dorchester, Wicomico, Somerset and Worcester counties, as well as on Assateague Island. The Maryland Department of Natural Resources identifies Henry's release of five or six animals as the start of the state's population.Few people could have expected such a small introduction to change the region's wildlife. Sika deer are smaller than native white-tailed deer and are often recognised by their dark coats and white spots, which they can retain into adulthood. They are comfortable in marshes, wetlands and wooded areas, habitats that are common along Maryland's lower Eastern Shore. Their ability to thrive in these habitats helped the animals move beyond James Island and onto the mainland. A later genetic study found that the modern Maryland population has relatively low genetic diversity, reflecting its origins from a very small number of founders. Even so, the deer have remained healthy and expanded their range.How a handful of deer spread across the Eastern ShoreThe population soon spread beyond James Island. Sika deer were soon reported on nearby parts of Dorchester County, and by the 1920s some of the animals were moved to Assateague Island. Four sika deer were introduced to Assateague Island in 1923 from a captive population in Cambridge, Maryland, according to the National Park Service. By the late 1960s, the island's population had grown to more than 1,000. (National Park Service)The deer also continued expanding on the mainland. Their preferred habitat helped them avoid some of the competition they might have faced with white-tailed deer in more open upland areas. Maryland wildlife managers later found that sika deer tended to spend much of their time in marshes, swamps and wet woodlands rather than using exactly the same areas as white-tailed deer. That reduced direct competition between the two species, though concerns remained where their ranges overlapped.Assateague became one of the best-known places to see the introduced deer. The island is famous for its wild horses, but sika deer also became a regular part of its wildlife. They live in the island's forests and salt marshes and can sometimes be seen moving between vegetation and open areas. The National Park Service describes them as a non-native species introduced during the 1920s. Their presence has also created a management challenge because the same habitats support native wildlife and vegetation.What makes the story unusual is the contrast between the tiny original release and the deer’s later range. The first animals did not arrive as a large herd. A few deer reproduced; some were moved to new locations, and their descendants gradually occupied suitable habitat. That pattern has been seen with other introduced species, but deer are large animals, so their spread is easier for people to notice once populations become established.A popular game animal with a complicated legacySika deer eventually became popular with hunters, particularly in Dorchester County and on Assateague Island. Their arrival also created a management question that Maryland continues to deal with: how many should remain, and where should their numbers be controlled? Wildlife managers have used hunting to keep populations at levels that balance recreational hunting with concerns about agricultural damage, habitat and competition with native deer.Sika deer are now an established part of Maryland's lower Eastern Shore, and hunting them has become an important recreational activity. At the same time, they are still an introduced species, and managers have to consider their effects on plants and other wildlife. A population that began with only a few animals can become difficult to control once it spreads through marshes, forests and agricultural areas.The Maryland population began with roughly five or six deer, yet the animals eventually spread through four counties and became established on Assateague Island. Another four were deliberately introduced on Assateague in 1923, helping establish the island's population. Their story shows how misleading the size of an initial release can be.More than a century after the first Maryland release, sika deer are now established across part of the Eastern Shore. They occupy a much larger part of the Eastern Shore and have become a familiar sight on Assateague. What began with a handful of Japanese deer has therefore become a permanent part of Maryland's wildlife-management story: an introduced animal that found suitable habitat, multiplied and spread far beyond the place where people first put it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
