articles.title: The invisible war: Iran's evolving cyberattacks bring battlefront to small-town America
articles.summary: Middle East News: On February 28, the US and Israel unleashed Operation Roaring Lion. Dramatic footage of missiles striking military, nuclear and government targets acr.
articles.body: On February 28, the US and Israel unleashed Operation Roaring Lion. Dramatic footage of missiles striking military, nuclear and government targets across Iran was broadcast around the world.But as the physical assault unfolded, another battle raged in parallel — one with no fighter jets in the sky and no missiles streaking across the horizon.Coordinated cyberattacks tore through Iran’s networks, compromising news platforms and a popular prayer app, disrupting communications and replacing state television broadcasts with messages from Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu.The physical assault was visible to the world; the digital blitzkrieg was largely invisible.It was a glimpse of a new kind of warfare. And Iran fought back.Iranian cyberoperators and affiliated groups targeted US and Israeli systems, stole sensitive information and disrupted infrastructure, increasingly extending the conflict far beyond the Middle East.The latest warning came in July, when cyberattacks hit water and wastewater facilities across at least 12 US states, including more than 30 systems in Minnesota.US authorities have not conclusively attributed the attacks to Tehran, but Iranian-linked actors are among the suspects.CyberAv3ngers, which is affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), issued a release regarding cyberattacks; while APT IRAN, which is linked to CyberAv3ngers, declared in an August 11 statement on its Telegram channel: "The attack on Minnesota was the work of the CyberAv3ngers and us, and we take direct responsibility for it."We have carried out attacks on US infra, and we warn America to back down ... threatening Iran’s infra and shedding the blood of Iran's children has a very heavy price ... our intention in attacking Minnesota was only to warn ... US electricity, telecommunications, water is under our control, and whenever America acts arrogantly, we will press the buttonWhat began as a shadowy adjunct to conventional warfare is now a battlefield in its own right — one where the target may not be a military base, but the network controlling a water pump in small-town America.The physical war may be thousands of kilometres away. The cyberwar is already knocking on America’s door.The invisible warWithin the first hours of the 2026 US-Israeli strikes, multiple pro-regime Iranian news agencies were simultaneously compromised.Legitimate-looking but fabricated content was injected into their front pages, designed to degrade morale of pro-regime forces using classic PSYOPS tactics. The sites were quickly taken down and restored, but not before reaching a wide audience during the most critical early hours. By injecting content at the exact moment Iranians turned to state media for strike coverage, the attackers maximised psychological impact during the regime's most vulnerable window.The simultaneous compromise of multiple outlets suggests pre-positioned access – these intrusions were prepared well in advance and activated on cue.Shortly after, BadeSabaa, a popular Iranian prayer time app with over 30 million installations from the Iranian app store, was hijacked.Push notifications were sent to its entire user base, calling on army members to surrender and join the people if they wanted to survive.The target selection was precise. As a prayer time app, its users skew heavily religious and conservative, a demographic overlapping significantly with pro-regime supporters and military personnel.During the second day of strikes, Iranian national television's Channel 3 satellite streams on IntelSat were hijacked. Viewers were shown video broadcasts of speeches by Trump and Netanyahu instead of regular programming.In repsonse, Iran went into full internet blackout, not only as a reaction to the cyberattacks but to stifle any dissent, and control information reaching the public.Iran retaliatesIn the 6 months preceding the 2026 US-Iran war, the global distribution of cyberattacks reflected expected threat trends: the US led with 18% of all incidents, followed by India (6%), Israel (6%), Indonesia (5%), and Thailand (5%).But in the 24 hours following the February 28 strikes, the picture shifted dramatically.Israel jumped from 6% to 21% of global incidents – a 3.5x increase. Crucially, Gulf states such as UAE, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia appeared in the top 5 for the first time, reflecting retaliatory and spillover targeting linked to their proximity to the conflict and hosting of US military assets.Analysis of 179 threat incidents painted a clear picture of the hacktivist playbook.Denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks dominated at 37% of all incidents, consistent with hacktivist preference for high-visibility, low-effort disruption.But the data also revealed more concerning activities: 9 incidents involved compromise of security cameras and industrial control systems used to operate machinery and infrastructure in the US; alleged breaches of Israeli Defense Forces servers and Ministry of Defence data, and targeted data leaks of military personnel and civilian information.Iran had been preparing.A decade of cyber escalationThe invisible war did not start in 2026.The roots trace back to Stuxnet (2010), the US-Israeli cyberweapon that infiltrated industrial systems associated with Iran's nuclear programme and physically destroyed centrifuges at Natanz. The US also planned an effort known as Nitro Zeus, a programme to disrupt Iranian air defences, communications and power grid.Iran could not match the US aircraft for aircraft, missile for missile or carrier for carrier. But it could target the networks that connected financial institutions, telecommunications systems, industrial facilities and government agencies.The Iranian response evolved rapidly.In 2012, Iranian-linked actors were blamed for Operation Ababil, a campaign of distributed denial-of-service attacks against US banks. The attacks temporarily disrupted online banking services and demonstrated that Iran did not need to destroy a bank's physical infrastructure to impose costs on it.The same period saw the Shamoon attack against Saudi Aramco, in which data on thousands of computers was erased. US officials attributed the attack to Iran and launched counter cyberoperations.Between 2013 and 2017, Iran-based Mabna Institute targeted computer systems of 144 American universities and 42 private sector firms. The group may have stolen over 31 terabytes of academic data and intellectual property worth approximately $3.4bn, said the US Department of Justice.Over time, Tehran developed a broader ecosystem involving government organisations, military-linked cyber units, contractors and proxy groups.During the June 2025 12-Day War, cyberattacks surged 700% within 48 hours.Pro-Israel cybersabotage group Predatory Sparrow wiped data of Iran's state-owned Bank Sepah; and burned $90 million in Nobitex cryptocurrency.Over 100 pro-Iranian hacktivist groups mobilised on Telegram. Israel was the most targeted country by geopolitically motivated hackers in 2025, absorbing 12.2% of all global attacks.By February 2026, Iran was primed to use cyberwarfare to its asymmetric advantage.Iran's strike on StrykerOn March 11, US company Stryker suffered a major cyberattack that disrupted its global Microsoft environment.The Iran-linked Handala hacking group claimed responsibility and portrayed the operation as retaliation for the US-Israeli military campaign.Stryker confirmed that it had suffered a cyberattack and was experiencing a global network disruption. The attackers claimed they had wiped more than 200,000 systems and extracted 50 terabytes of data.The attack represented a major escalation because of what Stryker does.It is not a weapons manufacturer. It makes medical devices used by US hospitals.That makes the target strategically interesting. An attacker does not necessarily need to strike a hospital directly. Disrupting a company that supplies the healthcare system can create pressure further downstream.This is what makes modern cyberwarfare so difficult to contain.The target may be civilian. The consequences may be civilian. And the attacker can still regard the operation as part of a military campaign.US water system under cyberseigeFollowing the attack, the FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), National Security Agency and Environmental Protection Agency warned that Iranian-affiliated actors were exploiting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) across American critical infrastructure.PLCs are not glamorous pieces of technology. They are industrial computers that control physical processes: pumps, valves, motors, pressure systems and other machinery.That is precisely why they matter.Compromising a PLC means crossing the line from stealing data to potentially manipulating the physical world.The April advisory said Iranian-affiliated actors had already caused operational disruptions and financial losses, including configuration wiping, manipulation of mechanical sensors and disruption of human-machine interfaces.Then came the Minnesota incidents.Over 30 community water systems were targeted on July 26 and 27. Investigators have not publicly established Iranian responsibility, but the attacks resembled previous Iranian-linked intrusions into US water infrastructure.The attack expanded and eventually covered systems across at least 12 states.Some systems lost remote control, experienced pressure problems or had to revert to manual operations.The New York Times reported that at least 100 facilities across the US have been targeted, though the names and locations of these facilities were not released.The attacks were not catastrophic. But that is precisely what makes them significant.A missile strike announces itself. A cyberattack can be almost invisible until a pump stops working, a hospital's systems go offline, a company's computers are wiped or a mobile phone quietly reveals the location of a soldier.The SS7 exploit: From opportunistic hacking to wartime strategyPerhaps the most striking development is that Iran's cyber campaign is no longer limited to hacking computers.It is increasingly about exploiting the digital ecosystem around people.In July, reporting based on telecom data indicated that Iranian actors had exploited weaknesses in SS7, an old signalling protocol used by mobile networks, to track the locations of US military personnel and contractors in the Middle East.SS7 vulnerabilities have long been known. They can allow sophisticated actors to obtain information about where a mobile device is located.In this case, the reporting indicated that Iranian actors used telecom infrastructure and commercial advertising technology to locate US personnel in countries including Iraq and Bahrain. The information may have assisted subsequent attacks on US personnel, though the precise operational links remain difficult to establish.The implication is profound.A smartphone does not need to be hacked for it to become an intelligence source.The networks around it can be enough.The same is true of cameras, advertising platforms, cloud services, internet-connected industrial equipment and corporate identity systems.Information warfareIran's cyber strategy is rooted in a broader doctrine of asymmetric warfare. Faced with conventionally superior US and Israeli military capabilities, Tehran has sought ways to impose costs without necessarily confronting those forces symmetrically.Cyber capabilities fit that strategy particularly well.Iranian actors have targeted local government systems, gas-station payment infrastructure and water facilities in the US. Pro-Iranian hacktivist groups have simultaneously targeted organisations across the Middle East. US and Israeli officials, military personnel and intelligence-linked individuals have also faced hack-and-leak operations.At first glance, these attacks can appear disconnected. A compromised government system, leaked personal information or disrupted infrastructure may seem to have little direct bearing on a war thousands of kilometres away.But their value can be measured in psychological and political terms.The objective is partly to demonstrate reach. If Iranian-linked operators can penetrate systems belonging to senior officials, military personnel or critical infrastructure, they can undermine the perception that those institutions are secure. That can have an effect disproportionate to the technical damage caused.The second objective is friction. Repeated cyber incidents can create uncertainty among businesses, governments and ordinary citizens. They generate a persistent sense that the conflict can reach into everyday life, even when no missiles are falling.This is where cyber operations become information warfare. Their physical effect may be limited, but their psychological effect can be amplified by social media, news coverage and public anxiety. Iran can therefore impose costs at a distance while attempting to shape how the conflict is perceived by domestic and international audiences.AI is making the cyber campaign faster and largerArtificial intelligence is adding another layer to this strategy.Recent threat-intelligence reporting indicates that Iranian actors have used AI across multiple stages of cyber and information operations, including reconnaissance, code and malware development, social engineering, and the creation and manipulation of content.AI has therefore not fundamentally altered Iran's strategic logic, but it has increased the speed, scale, reach and potential impact of its operations.The threat actors are conducting reconnaissance and capability development against PLC installations using AI-generated exploitation scripts disguised as legitimate monitoring toolsAI does not necessarily give Iran a revolutionary new weapon. Instead, it can make existing techniques more efficient. Reconnaissance can be accelerated, convincing social-engineering material can be produced at greater scale, and cyber operators can potentially develop or modify malicious code more quickly.For countries defending critical infrastructure, this means that the problem is not merely the sophistication of individual attacks. It is the possibility of a sustained volume of activity that continually tests weak points.The big pictureA war that began with missiles and airstrikes over Iran is increasingly being felt in places far removed from the Middle Eastern battlefield.And unlike a missile, the weapon may not arrive with a warning.What began largely as opportunistic disruption, espionage and hacktivist activity has increasingly become an integrated component of Iran’s broader war strategy, used not only to steal information or disrupt systems, but to support kinetic operations, influence perceptions and impose costs on adversaries far beyond the battlefield.Cyber operations thus function as an enabling layer across Iran's asymmetric strategy.The Strait of Hormuz and Iran's ability to disrupt energy flows remain much more powerful sources of leverage. Missiles, drones and economic pressure can produce more immediate physical effects. But cyber capabilities allow Tehran to extend that pressure into domains that are geographically distant and politically sensitive.For the United States, the challenge will be particularly acute as the conflict continues and the 2026 midterm elections approach. Iran has a history of targeting US elections and political campaigns, making cyber resilience increasingly important not only for critical infrastructure but also for the political system.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the life sentences of two convicts in the Bilkis Bano gang rape and murder case and granted them bail.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the life sentences of two convicts in the Bilkis Bano gang rape and murder case and granted them bail."Having heard the parties, suffice it to state that the appellants have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years, and also the fact remains that one of the appellants has a severe handicap. Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law," the apex court said in its October 28 order that has now been uploaded."In view of the above and considering the issues involved in this appeal, we suspend the sentence and grant bail to the appellants on such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the concerned trial court," the bench added.A Supreme Court bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale noted that Bilkis Bano case convicts Bipin Chandra Joshi and Pradeep Mordhiya had spent more than 17 years in prison.The two are among the 11 convicts whose remission was quashed by the apex court on January 8, 2024. Bano was five months pregnant when she was gang-raped during the 2002 Gujarat riots, while her three-year-old daughter and six other family members were killed.Also Read: Bilkis Bano gang rape case: All 11 life imprisonment convicts released under Gujarat government's remission policyThe other convicts in the case are: Govind Nai, Ramesh Chandana, Mitesh Bhatt, Bakabhai Vohania, Kesarbhai Vohania, Jaswant Nai, Radheshyam Shah, Rajubhai Soni and Shailesh Bhatt.The court had earlier struck down the Gujarat government's remission order, holding that Maharashtra had the authority to decide on their early release.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Telangana farmer dies in road accident, but SBI General Insurance rejects family's Rs 20 lakh personal accident claim over missing driving licence; consumer court records Rs 18 lakh settlement and directs insurer to pay within 30 days or face 9% interest
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A consumer commission in Telangana has directed SBI General Insurance to pay Rs 18 lakh to the family of a man who died in a road accident,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A consumer commission in Telangana has directed SBI General Insurance to pay Rs 18 lakh to the family of a man who died in a road accident, after the two sides settled a claim the insurer had rejected over a missing driving licence.In its November 11, 2026, order, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Warangal, recorded the settlement, which the family accepted as full and final, and directed payment within 30 days.Family’s insurance claimAccording to the commission order, Busa Komala, the wife of Busa Kumaraswamy, and his father, Busa Mallaiah, approached the commission after SBI General Insurance rejected their claim following his death in a road accident.Kumaraswamy, an agriculturist from Seetharampuram village, had a savings account with Telangana Grameena Bank, earlier known as Andhra Pradesh Grameena Vikas Bank. The bank had a tie-up with SBI General Insurance to provide personal accident insurance to its account holders.The complainants alleged that the bank had advised Kumaraswamy to take the policy as a pre-condition for crop loans and deducted the annual premium from his account. The last premium of Rs 1,000 was deducted on March 25, 2025.The insurer issued a policy with a sum assured of Rs 20 lakh, valid from March 25, 2025, to March 24, 2026. The family said it had no clause requiring a driving licence.According to the complaint, on May 24, 2025, Kumaraswamy was returning from a function on a motorcycle with a relative when a lorry hit their vehicle and he died on the spot. Police registered an FIR against the lorry driver and later filed a charge sheet.SBI General Insurance rejected the claim in a letter dated December 10, 2025, which said the documents did not meet policy requirements, cited the policy’s definition of “accident” and sought his driving licence.The family alleged deficiency in service and sought the Rs 20 lakh insured amount with 12 percent annual interest, Rs 2 lakh compensation and Rs 50,000 in litigation expenses.What did the bank and insurer say?Telangana Grameena Bank admitted that Kumaraswamy had an account with it and that it deducted the Rs 1,000 premium with his authorisation. It denied forcing him to take the policy and said it had no knowledge of the accident, the rejection or the licence.SBI General Insurance said the family failed to submit mandatory documents, particularly the licence, despite reminders. It argued that driving without a valid licence violated the Motor Vehicles Act, the policy was not a motor insurance policy, and the claim could not be kept pending indefinitely.Settlement and orderThe bench of president G Nagaraju and member V Janardhan Reddy noted that when the case was listed for the insurer’s evidence, the two sides filed a joint memo agreeing to settle the claim for Rs 18 lakh as full and final payment, Rs 2 lakh less than the insured amount claimed. They said the settlement was reached without undue influence, coercion and misrepresentation.The commission did not rule on whether the rejection was justified or whether a driving licence could be demanded. It also gave no reasons for dismissing the claim against the bank.“In view of the above factual position, this Commission inclined to dispose of the matter with a direction to the Opposite Party No.2 (in view of the matter settled amicably outside the Commission) to pay an amount of Rs.18,00,000/- towards full and final settlement within (30)days from today, failing which it shall carry interest at 9 percent from the date of default till its realization and there will not be any future claims. The claim against the Opposite Party No.1 is dismissed,” the commission concluded.Final orderThe commission directed SBI General Insurance to:Pay Rs 18 lakh towards full and final settlement within 30 days, with no future claims.Pay 9 percent annual interest from the date of default if it misses the deadline.The complaint against Telangana Grameena Bank was dismissed.

articles.title: Modi meeting, rare Putin-Xi talks: What’s on Trump’s Asia agenda amid poll setback & Nvidia row
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump is set to begin his Asia trip on Monday, with meetings with regional leaders, trade deals and a first-ever three-way discussion
articles.body: US President Donald Trump is set to begin his Asia trip on Monday, with meetings with regional leaders, trade deals and a first-ever three-way discussion on nuclear weapons with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the agenda. The visit will take him to Manila in the Philippines before he travels to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.The Manila leg is also drawing attention over a possible meeting between Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, as well as discussions around a Quad leaders' summit involving India, the US, Japan and Australia.It comes as Trump faces domestic political challenges after his party lost both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections, while a controversy involving chipmaker Nvidia has added scrutiny to his administration's China policy.The trip will also put Trump in the spotlight over his administration's handling of Nvidia-related export restrictions and its approach to China. The president is expected to discuss nuclear stockpiles with Xi and Putin, while the White House has said he plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand during his Philippines visit.Will Trump meet Modi in Manila?The possibility of a meeting between PM Modi and Trump has drawn attention amid preparations for the Manila visit and discussions about a possible Quad leaders' summit. The grouping brings together India, the US, Japan and Australia.US secretary of state Marco Rubio had indicated last month that a Quad summit was planned alongside the wider meetings in the Philippines. However, ministry of external affairs (MEA) has said it has no confirmed information about the summit or a possible meeting between the two leaders.Any interaction between PM Modi and Trump would come as India and the US continue trade negotiations.In Manila, Trump is also expected to meet Southeast Asian leaders, who look to Washington for support in countering China's growing assertiveness in the region. The White House has said he plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand during the visit.Rare Putin-Xi-Trump talks to focus on nuclear stockpilesThe most significant diplomatic event of the trip is expected at its conclusion, when Trump will hold the first-ever three-way talks with Xi and Putin. US officials have indicated that the discussions will focus on the three countries' nuclear weapons stockpiles.The talks are not expected to cover Russia's war in Ukraine, which is now in its fifth year, according to US officials cited by news agency AP. Trump has recently spoken about the possibility of a settlement to the conflict.The ongoing US war with Iran is also likely to form part of the wider geopolitical backdrop to the meeting. Iran has often aligned itself with China and Russia. The conflict has also been widely blamed for contributing to the Republican Party's losses in the midterm elections.China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the proposed trilateral talks as being of “groundbreaking significance” on Monday. She said Beijing wanted to hold in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting stability.“Under the current circumstances, the three countries shoulder an important responsibility to work together in addressing global challenges,” she said at a regular briefing in Beijing, as quoted by AP.Nvidia controversy to shadow Trump’s China visitThe Nvidia controversy is expected to remain a point of scrutiny during Trump's visit to China, even as US officials have sought to play down the issue. The row centres on the company's links to Jensen Huang and questions over the US administration's handling of export restrictions on its chips.The controversy intensified after Huang resigned as CEO last week following an admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has denied involvement in the matter.US officials have said Trump does not plan to raise the issue with Xi during their meeting. articles.title: A New York woman says she tended a strip of land less than two feet wide beside her home for 29 years, but her neighbours dispute her ownership claim; a judge has allowed the property lawsuit to proceed
articles.summary: A New York woman who says she has cared for a thin strip of land next to her house for almost 30 years can move forward with a lawsuit over who owns it,
articles.body: A New York woman who says she has cared for a thin strip of land next to her house for almost 30 years can move forward with a lawsuit over who owns it, despite her neighbors trying to stop her claim. The strip of land is only 18 to 24 inches wide, yet it runs about 165 feet along the line between the two yards. Lauren Sullivan says she has used, cared for, and improved the space for around 29 years, arguing that taking care of the land for so long gives her the legal right to own it. Her neighbors, Lisa Walts and John Walts III, disagree, saying the issue is just a small border mistake involving a chain-link fence.In a ruling dated 12 November 2026, New York Supreme Court Justice Elizabeth Snyder Fortino refused to throw out Sullivan's lawsuit and turned down the neighbors' request to decide the case right away without a full trial, known as summary judgment. This lets the fight continue so the court can look closer at the facts. The ruling does not mean Sullivan owns the land; instead, it means her claims raise enough legal and factual questions to keep the case going. The decision was posted on Justia as Sullivan v Walts, under the citation 2026 NY Slip Op 51905(U).Dispute centres on a narrow boundary stripAccording to Sullivan's lawsuit, the land in question sits right along the shared border of the two homes in Oneida County, New York. She states that she has controlled the strip openly, on her own, and without a break for about 29 years, keeping up and improving the space while treating it as part of her own yard. Sullivan is asking the court to declare her the owner under Article 15 of New York's Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law (RPAPL). Her case relies on a legal rule called adverse possession, which lets a person gain legal ownership of land after using it for a set number of years under specific rules.The lawsuit also includes separate complaints for trespassing and private nuisance. Sullivan claims that building work done by her neighbors got in the way of her property and pushed rainwater runoff onto her yard, making up her first legal complaint separate from the fight over who owns the strip. The neighbors challenged the land ownership claim before they even filed their official response to the lawsuit. According to the court's summary, they argued that Sullivan only mowed the grass, planted flowers, and did basic upkeep on the small strip, stating that these simple tasks are not enough to win ownership under New York law.Neighbours challenge ownership claimTo back up their side, the neighbors used a land survey dated 15 July 2026, made by Bradley G. Pcolinsky. As noted in the court ruling, the survey showed that Sullivan's chain-link fence went past the official property line and onto a thin piece of the neighbors' yard. The neighbors also handed in photos and a sworn written statement describing the strip, proving that there were no major buildings or upgrades on the land besides a four-foot chain-link fence. They argued that cutting grass, planting flowers, and doing normal yard work do not count as the type of control needed to gain ownership through adverse possession. The court agreed that New York judges have turned down ownership claims based only on small border crossings or basic yard care, yet Justice Fortino said the proof shown so far is not enough to end the fight at this early point.What the law says about adverse possessionUnder the version of New York's adverse possession law that applies to Sullivan's case, anyone trying to claim land must prove several things. Their use of the land must be without permission, under a claim of right, actual, open for all to see, exclusive to them, and unbroken for the required number of years. If the person does not have a written deed for the land, they must also prove the space was usually farmed, improved, or blocked off by a solid fence or wall. The court pointed to past cases, including Walling v Przybylo (2006) and Estate of Becker v Murtagh (2012), to explain these legal rules.Sullivan specifically states that her ownership rights were locked in before changes to Article 5 of the RPAPL took effect in 2008. This detail matters because the judge has to use the laws that were in place during the years Sullivan says she earned ownership. Justice Fortino decided that Sullivan had properly listed all the needed parts of an adverse possession claim in her initial paperwork. However, writing a valid complaint is different from proving a case in court, and Sullivan will still have to back up her claims with clear and convincing proof at trial.Judge says more evidence is neededA main reason the judge let the case continue was that the court did not yet have all the facts. Justice Fortino noted that several big questions still needed answers, including when the chain-link fence was put up, who built it, and whether past owners of both homes treated it as the true property line. The court also said it was not clear how much work or improvement Sullivan had actually done on the strip over the decades, or whether she had permission to use the land or took it over without asking. This difference matters because simply using or caring for someone else's yard does not automatically make it yours. The judge also questioned whether the strip was farmed or improved enough to meet the old law's rules, and whether the chain-link fence counts as a solid enclosure.To explain why more digging was needed, the court looked at Estate of Becker v Murtagh, which had proof of decades of upkeep, landscaping, building, and other actions that matched true ownership. The judge also looked at a 2026 Court of Appeals ruling involving the Genesee County Fish and Game Protective Association, where the group proved long-term care of a disputed road by plowing, paving, patching, and fixing it. Justice Fortino pointed out that Sullivan's case is different because the two sides have not yet gone through the formal evidence-gathering phase, called discovery. The judge noted that Sullivan has not yet been questioned under oath, and the court has not heard from past owners of the homes, meaning the court cannot yet decide if her yard work is enough to win ownership.Trespass and nuisance claims also surviveThe fight over who owns the strip is not the only part of Sullivan's lawsuit moving forward. Even though the neighbors mostly targeted her land ownership claim, Justice Fortino also reviewed her claims of trespassing and private nuisance. Sullivan states that construction next door interfered with how she uses and enjoys her yard, and she says the neighbors pushed surface water onto her land. The judge ruled that these claims were strong enough to stay in the lawsuit. Again, this ruling does not mean the neighbors actually trespassed or caused a nuisance, as those issues will be settled later in the case just like the land ownership fight.What happens next in the case?In the 12 November order, Justice Fortino denied the neighbors' request to dismiss the case under CPLR 3211(a)(7), refused to turn their dismissal request into a summary judgment request, and denied their separate request for summary judgment under CPLR 3212. The court ordered Sullivan to mail a copy of the ruling and a formal notice to the neighbors' lawyer, and to file proof of that mailing by 18 November 2026. The neighbors must then file their official response to the lawsuit within 10 days after getting those papers.After that response is filed, both sides must fill out and turn in a planning schedule by 9 December 2026, or show up in court for a planning meeting on 21 December 2026 at 2pm if they miss that deadline. This next phase will help both sides gather the proof needed to settle their different stories about how the thin strip of land was used and cared for. For now, the court has not decided who owns the land, leaving Sullivan with the job of proving her claim while her neighbors keep the right to fight her evidence as the lawsuit moves ahead.You use AI every day. articles.title: A decade out of power: Why Congress is struggling to make a comeback in Uttarakhand
articles.summary: \"If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.
articles.body: "If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat. If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will succumb in every battle."The 'Art of War' by Sun Tzu seems to perfectly encapsulate what Congress needs to understand for the upcoming Uttarakhand assembly elections.The BJP, led in the state by chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, is seeking a historic third consecutive term. At a recent event in Dehradun, Union home minister Amit Shah set an ambitious target of winning more than 65 of the state's 70 assembly seats. The Congress, meanwhile, hopes to capitalise on dissatisfaction with the government and return to power after a decade in opposition.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();On paper, the Congress has a substantial list of issues to take to voters. The BJP, too, faces the challenge of defending its record in a state where the pendulum of power had previously been in constant swing.But the electoral arithmetic presents a more complicated picture as we saw in 2022. BJP can lose ground and still win comfortably; Congress can make gains and still remain distant from power.So, can Congress turn voter dissatisfaction into a legitimate political direction, or will it simply reiterate its criticisms and fail to make waves?A state that once voted out its governmentsSince the state was formed in 2000, its first four assembly elections produced a change of government every five years. The Congress won 36 seats in 2002, the BJP secured 35 in 2007, the Congress edged ahead with 32 against the BJP's 31 in 2012, and the BJP swept to power with 57 seats in 2017.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();And then came 2022, an election that broke the pattern and highlighted BJP’s growing strength in the state. BJP won 47 of the state's 70 seats, becoming the first party to secure consecutive terms since Uttarakhand's formation.But Congress had also made gains. Compared to 2017, its performance had improved from 11 seats to 19, while its vote share rose from approximately 33.5 per cent to nearly 38 per cent.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The 2024 Lok Sabha election reinforced the challenge, with the BJP winning all five parliamentary constituencies in Uttarakhand. More significantly, Congress trailed in 63 of the state's 70 assembly segments, including 14 of the 19 constituencies it had won in 2022.Following the defeat, the Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee tasked former minister Nav Prabhat with assessing the party's performance. The preliminary assessment identified a familiar set of problems: infighting, poor communication and a lack of coordination among party leaders.Congress had conducted similar reviews after its defeats in the 2014 and 2019 Lok Sabha elections and the 2017 and 2022 assembly elections. Yet the organisational weaknesses identified in those exercises continued to surface.The Harish Rawat questionHarish Rawat remains one of Congress's most recognisable figures in Uttarakhand, but his prominence has also been tied to the party's internal power struggles.Rawat was overlooked for the chief minister's post in 2002, despite the party emerging as the largest formation. After returning to power in 2012, Congress was hit by a major crisis in 2016, when nine MLAs rebelled against his government, triggering President's Rule and a prolonged political and legal battle. Several rebels later joined the BJP.The mistrust has persisted in the run-up to 2027. The controversy involving Gaurav Kumar, an alleged conman posing as Rahul Gandhi's private secretary, exposed tensions within the state unit. Bhavna Pandey alleged that Kumar demanded Rs 2–3 crore, claiming the central leadership wanted state president Ganesh Godiyal replaced. Godiyal alleged a conspiracy, while Rawat denied any political plot and called for a police probe.Personal rivalries, including Rawat's falling-out with former aide Ranjeet Rawat, have added to the uncertainty. The November reshuffle distributed key responsibilities among senior leaders, but whether it can contain competing ambitions remains unclear.Congress's challenge is to draw on Harish Rawat's experience and support base without allowing the campaign to become another contest over leadership.Congress has plenty of issues, but no clear messageThe Congress has sought to make women's safety and accountability central to its criticism of the government. Garima Mehra Dasauni, the party's chief spokesperson in Uttarakhand, said Congress has compiled a list of alleged crimes against women involving senior BJP leaders in the state.Dasauni also argues that the BJP's electoral success cannot be understood simply through its development claims.In her assessment, religious and communal mobilisation, alongside welfare measures, has helped the party consolidate support. She also points to the political value of ration distribution and other welfare schemes, particularly among economically vulnerable households.This raises an important question for the Congress: how does it challenge welfare politics without appearing to dismiss the benefits that people receive?Welfare politics is not new to the Congress either. The National Food Security Act, which made access to subsidised foodgrains a legal entitlement, was enacted in 2013 under the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance government. However, the BJP has made welfare delivery a key component of its electoral strategy, raising questions about how the Congress can distinguish its own welfare agenda from that of the ruling party.The challenge for Congress, political observers suggest, is not a shortage of issues to raise but the absence of a common thread that ties them together and presents voters with a clear alternative.Political scientist Hilal Ahmed explains:"The Congress is raising all these issues but they lack a narrative between them. What connects their concerns? BJP can easily answer all these separate claims."For the Congress, this creates a difficult strategic choice. It must distinguish itself from the BJP, but it cannot assume that voters will automatically respond to a campaign built around governance failures and economic grievances.Ahmed describes the Congress as having “a little bit of a victimhood mentality” and calls it “intellectually weak”. He also warns that its response to the BJP remains fragmented rather than forming a coherent and constructive critique.His assessment of the potential electoral consequences is stark: “BJP might not win but neither will Congress.”The BJP's advantageThe BJP's position in Uttarakhand is stronger than the Congress's current organisational condition. Combining the appeal of PM Modi, CM Dhami’s work on ground and the promise of continuity through the double-engine government, it seeks to retain its position.The BJP will also seek to hold together a broad social coalition, while appealing to women, young voters, ex-servicemen and the Sikh community. Its reported plans for younger candidates and greater emphasis on local feedback suggest an effort to refresh its organisation.At the same time, the party is linking voter-list revision to its rhetoric around identity and belonging. At a Dehradun meeting, BJP leader Bhatt urged workers to remove those described as “infiltrators”, saying: “Only the original people of Devbhoomi should decide the government.”The economic questionOne of the most important arguments in Ahmed's analysis concerns the state's economic and social structure.Migration is not simply a consequence of unemployment; it also reflects the concentration of education, healthcare, transport and jobs in towns and the plains.Ahmed argues that Congress has failed to develop a convincing response to the BJP's rhetoric around identity. It could challenge the government's economic priorities and what he describes as a decade of policy paralysis, but must offer more than general claims about unemployment.The BJP's vulnerabilities, and Congress's opportunityThe Dhami government's record offers Congress several openings: the Ankita Bhandari case and continuing questions over the alleged VIP angle, recruitment paper leaks, unemployment, migration, land rights and allegations of corruption.But identifying these vulnerabilities is easier than turning them into electoral support. Congress must show how it would address them, particularly concerns over employment, regional inequality and the protection of local land rights. The Uttarakhand Kranti Dal's attempt to revive the politics of statehood could also put pressure on Congress to articulate a stronger regional agenda.The party has begun preparing through leadership meetings, multiple Parivartan Yatras, village outreach and a campaign against the government's record.As Ahmed argues, Congress also has a lot of “professional politicians” — leaders who pursue political stature and may abandon Congress in the face of defeat, a scenario reminiscent of 2016.What will decide 2027?The BJP is approaching the election with the advantages of incumbency and a well-established organisation, but it is not without vulnerabilities.The Congress, meanwhile, has a substantial list of issues with which to challenge the government. But none of these issues will automatically produce a victory.The Congress needs to answer three questions.Who leads the party in Uttarakhand?What is its political alternative?Can it rebuild its organisation?The art of war is also the art of elections. The Congress is yet to demonstrate that it understands both itself and its electoral 'enemy'.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ludhiana man lands in hospital after eating rotis made from expired atta bought for Rs 682, store offers Rs 2,000 to settle; consumer commission orders refund with 8% interest and Rs 20,000 compensation, bars retailer from selling expired products
articles.summary: LUDHIANA: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Ludhiana, has held a retail chain store liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade
articles.body: LUDHIANA: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Ludhiana, has held a retail chain store liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practices for allegedly selling expired wheat flour to a customer, leading to health complications.According to the complaint, Kuldeep Kumar, a resident of Bhamian Khurd in Ludhiana and originally from Moga, purchased two 10-kg bags of Whole Wheat Chakki Atta from the retail outlet on Chandigarh Road, Ludhiana, on May 22, 2026, for Rs 682. After consuming rotis prepared from the flour, he reportedly developed a stomach infection. He was admitted to Civil Hospital, Ludhiana, where he underwent treatment. Doctors reportedly told him that the infection had been caused by consuming contaminated food.The complainant immediately checked the wheat flour and found that it had expired on May 10, 2026. He alleged that the store had failed to remove the expired product from its shelves and sold it without informing him of its expiry date.He further claimed that despite bringing the matter to the store's notice, its representatives neither addressed his complaint nor admitted any fault. Instead, they allegedly threatened him and even offered him Rs 2,000 to settle the matter. The complainant said he had suffered health complications due to the deficiency in service and unfair trade practices of the opposite parties.He sought directions from the commission for the opposite parties to pay Rs 2 lakh towards the claim amount, Rs 2 lakh as compensation and Rs 22,000 towards litigation expenses.The consumer commission noted that the retailer had failed to contest the complaint despite being served notices and was therefore proceeded against ex parte. Relying on documentary evidence, including the purchase invoice, photographs of the product and medical records, the commission observed that the acts and omissions of the opposite parties had not only caused health problems and monetary loss to the complainant but had also resulted in mental agony and shock.It held that the opposite parties were guilty of deficiency in service and had adopted unfair trade practices.A bench comprising Sanjeev Batra, President, and Monika Bhagat, Member, partly allowed the complaint and directed the opposite parties to refund the price of one bag of expired atta, along with 8% annual interest from the date of purchase. The commission also awarded the complainant a composite compensation of Rs 20,000.The order stated that the retailer must comply within 30 days, failing which it would be liable to pay Rs 200 per day, subject to a maximum penalty of Rs 10,000. The commission also directed the company to discontinue such unfair trade practices and restrained it from selling, displaying or offering expired products for sale.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Ludhiana | Silver Rate in Ludhiana | Bank Holidays in Ludhiana | Public Holidays in Ludhiana | Petrol Price in Ludhiana | Diesel Price in Ludhiana | CNG Price in Ludhiana | LPG Price in LudhianaStay updated with the latest Ludhiana news. articles.title: 'Significance can't be overstated': Kremlin on Putin-Trump-Xi meet, leans into Yalta comparison
articles.summary: The heads of state of Russia, the United States and China will meet in China on November 19 for a trilateral discussion that the Kremlin expects will have
articles.body: The heads of state of Russia, the United States and China will meet in China on November 19 for a trilateral discussion that the Kremlin expects will have a major impact on global affairs.Moscow has invoked the three countries' alliance during World War II and their role in establishing the United Nations, saying the meeting's significance and symbolism cannot be overstated.Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks would take place at Chinese President Xi Jinping's official residence in Shenzhen."The significance and symbolism of this meeting cannot be overstated. It is the first such meeting of its kind," Ushakov told reporters.The meeting is drawing comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the "Big Three", US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, met in Crimea to discuss the post-war order in Europe. The conference shaped the political settlement after World War II, including the division of Germany and the future of Eastern Europe.Ushakov said the meeting would be structured around the understanding and alliance shared by the three countries during the Second World War. He said the discussions would also focus on their cooperation in establishing the United Nations.He said the three countries were prepared to build on these historical ties and hold a substantive discussion."We believe that [the discussion] should have a significant impact on the development of the international situation as a whole," Ushakov said.The Kremlin said intensive consultations were underway on the text of a proposed joint statement. Moscow expects the three leaders to issue a joint communique after the meeting.Ushakov said that even if the three sides fail to agree on a joint statement, each leader will present his own assessment of the discussions.Putin and Xi will also hold a separate bilateral meeting on November 18, a day before the trilateral discussions, the Kremlin said.The talks will focus on prospects for economic cooperation between Russia and China, the Ukraine conflict and the Korean Peninsula. Ushakov said Putin would brief Xi on his contacts with the United States, including discussions held in Abu Dhabi.The trilateral meeting will take place as China hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.You use AI every day. articles.title: Five years after surviving the attack that killed her husband, Haiti's former first lady Martine Moise has registered for the country's first presidential election in a decade, joining 32 other hopefuls
articles.summary: Martine Moise, the widow of assassinated Haitian president Jovenel Moise, has registered to run in Haiti’s first presidential election in a decade,
articles.body: Martine Moise, the widow of assassinated Haitian president Jovenel Moise, has registered to run in Haiti’s first presidential election in a decade, according to Reuters and the country’s electoral council website. Her candidacy adds a deeply symbolic name to a contest that will take place amid a continuing security crisis, political instability, and widespread public frustration with the country’s leadership.Five years after her husband was killed in an attack at their home in July 2021, Moise is among 33 presidential hopefuls registered for an election currently scheduled for July next year. The vote would be Haiti’s first since 2016, following years of postponed elections as armed groups expanded their influence across much of the country.A candidacy shaped by lossMartine Moise was seriously wounded in the attack that killed her husband, who was president at the time. His assassination marked a major turning point for Haiti, deepening an already fragile political situation and leaving the country without an elected president.Her decision to enter politics will inevitably draw attention to that history. As the widow of the country’s last elected president, she carries both personal experience of the violence that reshaped Haiti and a political identity closely linked to her husband’s presidency.The electoral council’s website listed her registration among the candidates for the upcoming vote. Reuters reported that 33 people, including Moise, had registered for the presidential election.An election delayed for yearsHaiti last held an election in 2016. Since then, successive leaders have repeatedly postponed votes, citing insecurity and the growing power of armed gangs.The delays have left many Haitians without a direct national vote for nearly a decade. The country has faced overlapping crises involving gang violence, political turmoil, economic hardship, and weakened public institutions.The election is currently scheduled for July next year. Whether it proceeds as planned will depend on the government’s ability to organise voting in a country where armed groups control large areas and security remains a central concern.Why Moise’s entry mattersMoise’s candidacy is likely to test whether Haitian voters see her as a unifying figure or as part of the political establishment they want to move beyond. Her connection to Jovenel Moise gives her national recognition, but it also ties her campaign to the political period that preceded the country’s latest crisis.For supporters, her entry may represent continuity and a call to restore democratic institutions. For critics, it may raise questions about whether a new election can deliver the change many Haitians have been seeking.Her candidacy also brings international attention to a vote that could shape Haiti’s political future. With 33 registered candidates, the election will give voters a wide field to choose from, but the main issues will likely remain security, governance and rebuilding public trust.A nation on the brinkHaiti’s upcoming presidential election comes as the country continues to grapple with years of instability. The assassination of Jovenel Moise, the rise of armed groups, and repeated electoral delays have left many citizens questioning whether the political system can function.Martine Moise’s registration does not guarantee that the election will proceed smoothly. It does, however, give the vote a prominent contender with a personal history closely connected to the events that brought Haiti to its current moment.As the campaign develops, her platform, alliances, and ability to connect with voters will matter as much as her family name. For now, her candidacy signals that Haiti’s first presidential election in a decade will be one of the country’s most consequential political contests in years.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi got emotional while speaking about his mother, Sonia Gandhi, at the launch of her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, recalling her courage, resilience and the personal tragedies she has faced over the years.Speaking at the event, Rahul said the book offered a glimpse of his mother before the death of his father, former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi. He said Sonia had gone through several difficult phases in life but had never allowed them to break her spirit.“I have never seen her scared. I have never seen her back down,” Rahul said, praising her strength. He also revealed that Sonia was a four-time cancer survivor, adding that she often played down the seriousness of her health struggles.Rahul said he believed Rajiv Gandhi would have been proud of Sonia and the way she had dealt with the challenges in her life."The reason I wanted to give this speech is because, Mummy, Papa loved you, but I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you...", he said at the event.His remarks came as the family and several political leaders gathered to mark the release of the memoir, which reflects on Sonia’s personal journey, family life and years in public life.Meanwhile, BJP leader Captain Amarinder Singh, who was also present at the launch, praised the book. He said, “It is a wonderful book; I read it... It is a very well-written book.”Asked whether he would rejoin the Congress, Singh ruled it out, saying, “No... articles.title: Trump hints at meeting Kim Jong Un in China, says Xi could play role
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump on Monday raised the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China this week, introducing an unexpected
articles.body: US president Donald Trump on Monday raised the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China this week, introducing an unexpected diplomatic prospect into his trip to East Asia.Trump said the meeting could take place during his visit to China, but indicated that it would depend on whether Kim was willing to attend and on Chinese President Xi Jinping's role.Speaking to reporters at the White House before leaving for the Philippines and China, Trump said he could meet Kim alongside his planned engagements with Xi and Russian president Vladimir Putin.“We may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said. “So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot.”The possibility of another meeting comes despite earlier indications from senior US officials that Trump had no immediate plans to engage with the North Korean leader. The two have met several times during Trump's first presidency, between 2017 and 2021, including at the Korean Demilitarized Zone.Previous attempts to revive talksTrump has repeatedly expressed interest in meeting Kim again during his second term. However, previous hints about a possible encounter have not translated into talks. He also floated the prospect of meeting the North Korean leader during an Asia visit last year, but no meeting took place.North Korea has publicly indicated that it has no intention of meeting the US president at present. Its mission to the United Nations did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump's latest remarks.Trump said any meeting with Kim would take place in China, suggesting that Xi could play a role in facilitating the encounter. It remains unclear whether the North Korean leader has agreed to attend.Ukraine, Iran among issues on Trump's agendaTrump's East Asia trip will include meetings in the Philippines and China, with economic issues expected to feature prominently in his engagements in Manila. In China, he is expected to meet Xi, while a possible meeting with Putin has also been indicated.Trump and other officials have said discussions could cover Russia's war in Ukraine, counterproliferation and the conflict in Iran. However, US officials and analysts have played down expectations of a substantive agreement emerging from a possible trilateral meeting involving Trump, Xi and Putin.Trump said the trip would offer an opportunity to make progress on several issues, with further high-level engagements scheduled when the G20 summit is held in Miami in December.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Spent lakhs on a US master's, graduated with a 3.9 GPA, and still had to return to India': 26-year-old man earning Rs 9LPA asks, 'Did I not try hard enough'
articles.summary: Every American Dream story has a different ending. And some endings are dipped in introspection.
articles.body: Every American Dream story has a different ending. And some endings are dipped in introspection. A 26-year-old Indian man took to Reddit, questioning himself whether he had not tried hard enough to get a job in the US and pursue his American Dream. Instead, he had to return to India and settle for a Rs 9LPA job as an AI/ML engineer despite having an astounding academic record of a 3.9 GPA. The man said he graduated in May 2025 with a huge education loan burden."During my job search, I applied to hundreds of positions. I did get some interviews, but things didn't work out.
